title: Add local Otsu filter (`cucim.skimage.filters.rank.otsu`)
body:
## Summary

Adds `cucim.skimage.filters.rank.otsu`, the GPU version of
`skimage.filters.rank.otsu`: for every pixel, the gray level that maximizes the
between-class variance of the histogram of its neighborhood. It was one of the
two functions left out of the original `rank` module (the other is
`windowed_histogram`, which is not part of this PR).

```python
from cucim.skimage.filters.rank import otsu
local_threshold = otsu(image, footprint)
binary = image >= local_threshold
```

The signature is the same as the other generic rank filters
(`out`, `mask`, `shift_x/y/z`, `shifts`, `backend`, `cast_to_uint8`).
Input is uint8 or uint16; other dtypes are converted to uint8 by default, and
`cast_to_uint8=False` raises `ValueError` for them (the result is a histogram
bin index).

The result follows scikit-image's rules exactly: gray level 0 is never chosen,
only gray levels present in the neighborhood are candidates, a level that
already holds the whole neighborhood ends the search, the lowest level wins
ties, and a neighborhood with a single level (or no pixels) gives 0.

## Implementation

Two backends, selected by the existing `backend=` argument (`'auto'` by
default):

- **Elementwise** (any dimensionality, footprint, mask; uint8 and uint16).
  Each thread sorts its neighborhood and walks the runs of equal values, which
  are the occupied bins of the local histogram. The between-class variance is
  evaluated with the same operation order as scikit-image's `_kernel_otsu`,
  using explicit rounding (`__dmul_rn`, `__dsub_rn`, `__ddiv_rn`) so that the
  compiler cannot fuse operations.
- **Histogram** (2-D uint8, fully populated odd rectangular footprint, no
  mask, reflect mode, zero shift; used automatically from 15 x 15). This is a
  new operation in the existing sliding-histogram kernel
  (`cuda/histogram_rank.cu`). For every output pixel a 256-thread block holds
  the window histogram, one bin per thread, and:
  1. warp shuffles compute the prefix sums of the counts and of count * value
     (one block barrier combines the per-warp totals);
  2. every thread estimates the between-class variance of its bin in float,
     from exact 64-bit integer numerators (second barrier);
  3. the first warp finds the float maximum and evaluates, in double precision
     and in the reference's operation order, only the bins within 1e-5
     (relative) of it. The float error is below 1e-6, so the winner is the same
     as when every bin is evaluated in double; double precision division is
     slow on most GPUs, which is why it is limited to the few near-maximal
     bins. Chunks of 32 bins are visited in increasing order so the lowest bin
     wins ties.

  Only thread 0 uses the result, so no final broadcast is needed. The cost per
  pixel does not depend on the footprint size. The cutoff for `backend='auto'`
  is 15 x 15 (`_HISTOGRAM_MIN_FOOTPRINT_AREA['otsu']`): at 2048 x 2048 the two
  backends take 52 ms each for 15 x 15 on the camera image, and the elementwise
  backend is faster below that and slower above (on noise the cutoff is 13 x 13).

Other changes: `otsu` is added to the module docstring and `__all__` (it is
no longer listed as not implemented), and to the rank benchmarks
(`cucim_filters_rank_bench.py`, `run-nv-bench-filters-rank.sh`).

## Differences from scikit-image

- **Borders.** As for the other rank filters, cuCIM extends the image by
  reflection while scikit-image crops the neighborhood, so values within one
  footprint radius of the border can differ. The tests compare interior pixels
  with scikit-image and the full image with a brute-force reference that uses
  reflection.
- **Ties.** When two thresholds tie mathematically, which one wins depends on
  floating point rounding. scikit-image's own tests accept either value for
  such pixels (issue 3091), and so do these tests for pixels `[3, 5]`
  (41 or 81) and `[19, 18]` (141 or 172) of the reference data.
- **Huge windows.** The integer products are 64-bit, as in scikit-image's
  `Py_ssize_t`; windows of more than about 190 million pixels would overflow.

## Tests

Added to `rank/tests/test_rank.py` (64 new test cases; the whole file passes,
464 passed and 3 skipped for existing reasons):

- both backends against a brute-force reference for six images (camera,
  noise, few gray levels, binary, constant, zeros) and footprints 3, 7, 15
  and 31;
- scikit-image on interior pixels (2-D uint8 with both backends, uint16 with a
  non-square footprint, 3-D with a ball);
- disk footprint with and without a mask, windows with no unmasked pixel, an
  all-False footprint;
- histogram versus elementwise on a 41 x 41 window;
- scikit-image's two tie edge cases;
- `ValueError` for float input with `cast_to_uint8=False`;
- `otsu` in the existing reference-data, 3-D and dtype-comparison test lists,
  and the auto-backend cutoff.

## Performance

RTX A6000, Intel i9-10980XE, scikit-image 0.26.0, CuPy 14.2.0. GPU times are
the mean of 10 runs from `cupyx.profiler.benchmark` (after 3 warm-up runs); CPU
times are the best of 2 runs of `skimage.filters.rank.otsu` (1 run for images of
1 Mpixel or more). Images are tiles of `skimage.data.camera()`; uint16 and 3-D
inputs are random.

Square footprints, uint8, `backend='auto'`:

| Image | Footprint | scikit-image | cuCIM | Speedup | Backend |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 512 x 512 | 3 x 3 | 72.7 ms | 0.38 ms | 192x | elementwise |
| 512 x 512 | 7 x 7 | 113.4 ms | 0.88 ms | 129x | elementwise |
| 512 x 512 | 15 x 15 | 113.7 ms | 4.03 ms | 28x | histogram |
| 512 x 512 | 31 x 31 | 148.3 ms | 4.45 ms | 33x | histogram |
| 512 x 512 | 63 x 63 | 214.3 ms | 5.41 ms | 40x | histogram |
| 1024 x 1024 | 3 x 3 | 277.0 ms | 0.72 ms | 386x | elementwise |
| 1024 x 1024 | 7 x 7 | 368.8 ms | 2.25 ms | 164x | elementwise |
| 1024 x 1024 | 15 x 15 | 493.7 ms | 13.87 ms | 36x | histogram |
| 1024 x 1024 | 31 x 31 | 615.2 ms | 14.15 ms | 44x | histogram |
| 1024 x 1024 | 63 x 63 | 877.1 ms | 16.13 ms | 54x | histogram |
| 2048 x 2048 | 3 x 3 | 1098.3 ms | 1.87 ms | 587x | elementwise |
| 2048 x 2048 | 7 x 7 | 1461.2 ms | 7.71 ms | 190x | elementwise |
| 2048 x 2048 | 15 x 15 | 1799.5 ms | 50.95 ms | 35x | histogram |
| 2048 x 2048 | 31 x 31 | 2472.9 ms | 53.30 ms | 46x | histogram |
| 2048 x 2048 | 63 x 63 | 3616.1 ms | 56.69 ms | 64x | histogram |

Other cases (elementwise backend):

| Case | scikit-image | cuCIM | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| uint8 1024 x 1024, disk radius 3 | 356.7 ms | 1.50 ms | 237x |
| uint8 1024 x 1024, disk radius 7 | 462.5 ms | 8.50 ms | 54x |
| uint8 1024 x 1024, disk radius 15 | 616.3 ms | 59.13 ms | 10x |
| uint16 (12-bit) 512 x 512, 3 x 3 | 1119.2 ms | 0.39 ms | 2872x |
| uint16 (12-bit) 512 x 512, 7 x 7 | 1264.8 ms | 1.34 ms | 942x |
| uint16 (12-bit) 512 x 512, 15 x 15 | 1610.4 ms | 10.58 ms | 152x |
| uint8 128^3 volume, ball radius 1 | 787.9 ms | 1.09 ms | 726x |
| uint8 128^3 volume, ball radius 3 | 2696.4 ms | 17.47 ms | 154x |

Notes:

- The histogram backend takes about 51-57 ms at 2048 x 2048 for every footprint
  from 15 x 15 to 63 x 63, so the speedup grows with the footprint.
- A disk (or any non-rectangular footprint) cannot use the histogram backend,
  so large disks are the weakest case (10x at radius 15).
- The uint16 case is slow in scikit-image because it builds a 4096-bin
  histogram per window.
- The GPU timings do not include host-device transfers.

How the histogram backend got there (2048 x 2048 camera image, 15 x 15, GPU
time; during development): 99 ms with warp-shuffle prefix sums and every bin
evaluated in double, 145 ms with a float screening pass that was evaluated by
all threads, and 51 ms with the double-precision evaluation limited to the
first warp.

title: Add non-local means denoising
body:
## Description

This adds `cucim.skimage.restoration.denoise_nl_means`, a GPU implementation
of scikit-image's non-local means denoising with the same API.

- **Supported inputs.** Fast mode: 2D, 2D multichannel, 3D, 3D multichannel,
  4D and 4D multichannel. Slow mode (`fast_mode=False`): 2D, 2D multichannel and
  3D match scikit-image. scikit-image raises `NotImplementedError` for slow
  mode with 3D multichannel and 4D input; cuCIM computes these with the same
  kernels (documented in the `fast_mode` parameter; there is no scikit-image
  result to compare with, so these cases were validated separately, see
  "Validation beyond scikit-image" below, and slow mode is only modestly slower
  than fast mode: 1.0 to 1.6 times the fast mode time in float32 on an RTX
  A6000).
- **Matches scikit-image.** The patch weights and the cutoff checks are the
  same as in scikit-image. The largest observed difference from scikit-image is
  **1e-15 in float64** and **3.4e-7 in float32** on the configurations tested.
  This is an observation and not a guarantee: the floating point operations of
  the distances are in a different order, so a distance close to the cutoff can
  round to the other side and change which patches contribute, giving
  differences of the order of 1e-3 on small images (also in float64); this and
  the stricter argument checks are in the docstring. float32 images of very
  large or small magnitude are rescaled internally (for an unusual `h`).
- **Speed** on an RTX A6000, in float32: **~440–940× faster** than scikit-image
  in fast mode and **~9,600–11,800× faster** in slow mode (benchmarks below).
  On the GPU, slow mode costs only 1.05–1.5× as much as fast mode, so the
  original Gaussian-weighted algorithm becomes a practical choice.

### What "matching scikit-image" required

scikit-image's implementation has several details that affect results beyond
rounding. They are all reproduced here:

- **No real `exp`.** Every weight goes through `_fast_exp`, Schraudolph's
  approximation of the exponential. It is up to ~3% off from `exp`; for example
  `fast_exp(0) = 0.971`. The float64 kernels reproduce it bit for bit.
- **Fast mode's patch is `(s-1)^n`, not `s^n`.** scikit-image's integral-image
  distance sums over `[x - r + 1, x + r]` on each axis, which is asymmetric and
  one pixel short. It still normalizes by `s^n`. This looks like an off-by-one
  in scikit-image, so cuCIM adds an opt-in `symmetric_patch=True` that uses the
  centered patch instead (see below).
- **Slow mode's early exit.** The distance cutoff is tested on partial sums
  before each patch row (2D) or plane (3D), but not after the last one. When
  `sigma > 0` the partial sums are not monotonic, so testing only the final
  distance instead would change results (by up to 3.8e-3 in one test case).
- **Boundaries.** Slow mode clips the search window to the image; fast mode
  searches into the reflect-padded border.

## Kernels

scikit-image loops over half of the search window and scatters each pair's
weight to both pixels. On the GPU, both kernels use the equivalent **gather
form** instead: each output pixel sums over the full search window. That needs
no atomics, and results are deterministic.

### Direct kernel

- One thread per output pixel.
- For each shift in the search window, the thread computes the full patch
  distance from global memory and accumulates the weighted value in registers.
- Generic over 2D, 3D and 4D. It needs no shared memory, so it always works.

### Tiled kernel

- One thread block per output tile, with the loop over shifts inside the
  kernel. For each shift:
  1. **Phase A:** the block computes `Σ_c (u(y) − u(y+t))² − C·2σ²` over the
     tile plus the patch halo and stores it in shared memory. Each thread keeps
     the reference values for its own elements in registers, since they do not
     depend on the shift.
  2. **Phase B:** separable window sums along axes `ndim−1, …, 1`, each pass
     in shared memory. Fast mode uses box taps and slow mode Gaussian taps.
  3. **Phase C:** each thread sums along axis 0 for its own pixel,
     sequentially. This is where the slow-mode early exit is applied. The
     thread then computes the weight and accumulates it in registers.
- Each phase writes its own shared memory buffer. That leaves `ndim` barriers
  per shift and none at the end of a shift.
- Compared with the direct kernel, this cuts the work per pixel and shift by
  about 2× in 2D and 3–7.5× in 3D and 4D.

### No integral images

scikit-image's fast mode gets each patch distance from 4 (2D) or 8 (3D)
corners of a float64 integral image over the whole padded image, so its
rounding error grows with the image size. Both kernels here sum only the
`(s−1)^n` values of each patch, so the error does not depend on the image size.
This is also what makes float32 viable: a float32 integral image would lose all
precision on large images. Error of one shift's patch sums (s = 7), relative to
the sum of the patch's absolute values:

| Shape | float32, patch sums (cuCIM) | float32, integral image | float64, integral image (scikit-image) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 512² | 2.1e-7 | 2.9e-3 | 6.7e-12 |
| 2048² | 2.2e-7 | 4.0e-2 | 7.2e-11 |
| 8192² | 2.5e-7 | 1.0 | 1.7e-9 |
| 384³ | 2.3e-7 | 1.4e-1 | 3.0e-10 |

So for large images, the float64 results are slightly more accurate than
scikit-image's own.

### Padding and finalize

- **Padding.** The input is reflect-padded once into a planar
  `(C, *padded_shape)` buffer with cuCIM's vendored `pad`. Its single
  elementwise kernel also transposes channels-last input from a strided view.
  `cupy.pad` instead launches many small kernels; the vendored `pad` saves
  ~0.14 ms or more per call. The padding is extended to whole tiles, so the tiled
  kernel's inner loops need no bounds checks.
- **Finalize.** Sums the partial results when the search window is split
  across blocks (see below).

### Code generation

Both kernels are generated from Python string fragments, in the same style as
`filters/_separable_filtering.py`, and compiled with `cp.RawModule`. They are
memoized per device.

- **Compile-time constants:** ndim, number of channels, patch size, mode,
  float type, index type (`int` or `long long`, chosen by array size) and tile
  shape. All patch and channel loops are fully unrolled.
- **Runtime arguments:** `patch_distance`, `h`, `sigma`, shapes and strides.
- **`fast_exp`:** the double version is bit-identical to scikit-image's. The
  float version is built from integer and float32 operations only, avoiding
  FP64 math. It is within one 2^-20 quantization step of scikit-image's for
  every weight that passes the distance cutoff.
- **Accumulation:** float32 uses two-level summation (partial sums per row of
  shifts) to limit rounding growth.

## Kernel selection and launch configuration

The internal `kernel="auto"` setting (not a public parameter) works as follows:

1. **Direct kernel when there are fewer than 3 taps per axis**, i.e. fast mode
   with `patch_size` 3 (or 2, which becomes 3) and any mode with `patch_size`
   ≤ 1. With only two taps per axis, there is too little work per shift to
   amortize the tiled kernel's barriers. The direct kernel was 1.6–2.3× faster
   in 2D, 3D and 4D for these cases (table below).
   - For fast mode on single-channel 2D images, the threshold is 4 taps. This
     only affects `symmetric_patch=True` with `patch_size` 3, which has 3 unit
     taps; there the direct kernel was 1.2–1.6× faster (512² to 2048²,
     `patch_distance` 3–11). With 2 or more channels, in 3D and 4D, and for the
     3 Gaussian taps of slow mode, the tiled kernel was about as fast or faster.
2. **Otherwise the tiled kernel**, with default tiles `16×16` (2D), `8×8×8`
   (3D) and `4×4×4×4` (4D). These were the fastest in a tile-shape sweep.
3. **Shared memory check.** The tiled kernel needs
   `(Π(T_a + F − 1) + Σ_passes |part|) · itemsize` bytes of shared memory,
   where `F` is the number of taps per axis. If that exceeds the device's
   opt-in limit (99 KB on sm_86), the largest tile dimension is halved until it
   fits. Below 64 threads per tile the direct kernel is used instead. Requests
   above 48 KB set `max_dynamic_shared_size_bytes`.
4. **Splitting the search window for smaller images.** The launch aims for at
   least two waves of resident threads (`2 · SM count · max threads per SM`).
   With fewer blocks than that, the shifts along axis 0 are split into up to
   `2·patch_distance + 1` chunks, one per `gridDim.y` index.
   - Each chunk writes partial weighted sums and weight sums.
   - The finalize kernel adds the chunks in a fixed order and divides, so the
     result stays deterministic.
   - Both kernels use one thread per output pixel, so splitting applies to
     images with fewer pixels than two waves of resident threads: about 258k
     on the A6000, i.e. up to ~500² in 2D, ~63³ in 3D or ~22⁴ in 4D. Larger
     images run exactly as without splitting.

### Tiled vs direct

Time in ms, float32, RTX A6000, uniform random input (faster kernel in bold):

| Case | Tiled | Direct | Tiled speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2D 512², gray, fast, s=7, d=11 | **1.38** | 2.55 | 1.84× |
| 2D 512², RGB, slow, s=7, d=11 | **2.02** | 9.69 | 4.80× |
| 2D 1024², gray, fast, s=5, d=7 | **1.73** | 1.95 | 1.13× |
| 3D 96³, fast, s=5, d=5 | **14.98** | 45.85 | 3.06× |
| 3D 64³, slow, s=7, d=4 | **6.13** | 43.88 | 7.16× |
| 4D 20⁴, fast, s=5, d=2 | **4.42** | 28.07 | 6.36× |
| 2D 1024², gray, **fast, s=3**, d=7 | 1.53 | **0.67** | 0.44× |
| 3D 96³, **fast, s=3**, d=5 | 9.95 | **5.38** | 0.54× |
| 4D 24⁴, **fast, s=3**, d=2 | 3.10 | **1.95** | 0.63× |
| 2D 1024², gray, slow, s=3, d=7 | 1.88 | **1.77** | 0.94× |
| 2D 1024², RGB, slow, s=3, d=7 | **2.32** | 4.50 | 1.94× |
| 3D 96³, slow, s=3, d=5 | **13.19** | 25.40 | 1.93× |

Slow mode with `patch_size` 3 has 3 taps, so it uses the tiled kernel. That is
roughly break-even for single-channel 2D and ~1.9× faster for RGB or 3D.

## dtype handling and `compute_dtype`

- **Float type.** The working and output float type follows the cuCIM
  convention (as in the vendored ndimage code and `convert_to_float`):

  | Input dtype | cuCIM | scikit-image |
  |---|---|---|
  | float16, float32 | float32 | float32 |
  | bool, 8/16-bit integers | float32 | float64 |
  | float64, 32/64-bit integers | float64 | float64 |

- **New keyword `compute_dtype`** (cuCIM only). `None` (default) computes in
  the float type above. `float32` or `float64` forces that precision; the
  output dtype does not change.
  - Note that scikit-image's fast mode always computes in float64 internally.
  - Forcing float32 matters on GPUs with low FP64 throughput: on the RTX A6000
    the float64 path is ~10× slower.
  - Computing in float32 changes results by ≤ ~1.5e-6 relative to
    scikit-image's float64 result.

## `symmetric_patch` (cuCIM only)

scikit-image's fast mode looks up each patch distance from integral-image
corners at `x - r` and `x + r`. That sums over `(x - r, x + r]`, which is
`2r` elements per axis, offset by one from the centered `2r + 1` patch, while
the normalization uses `(2r + 1)^n`. A visible consequence is that the result
depends on the image's orientation. For a 48×48 test image (`patch_size=7`,
`patch_distance=5`, `h=0.3`), `denoise(flip(u))` and `flip(denoise(u))` differ
by up to 0.32 in scikit-image's fast mode. In slow mode they differ by 0.016,
from the row order of its early exit.

- **Default (`False`):** reproduces scikit-image.
- **`True`:** uses the centered `s^n` patch, like slow mode. The result is then
  flip-equivariant to rounding (~1e-15). It has no effect in slow mode.
- **Implementation:** only the patch's first tap offset and its tap count
  change (`F = s` instead of `s − 1`), so both kernels support it with no other
  changes. With 3 taps, `patch_size=3` uses the tiled kernel.
- **Cost** (float32, fast mode):

  | Case | Default | `symmetric_patch=True` |
  |---|---|---|
  | 2D 512², s=7, d=11 | 1.45 ms | 1.55 ms (1.07×) |
  | 2D 1024², s=5, d=7 | 1.66 ms | 1.89 ms (1.14×) |
  | 2D 512² RGB, s=7, d=11 | 1.88 ms | 2.04 ms (1.08×) |
  | 3D 64³, s=5, d=5 | 5.00 ms | 6.13 ms (1.23×) |
  | 3D 96³, s=7, d=5 | 25.9 ms | 31.4 ms (1.21×) |

- **Tests:** comparison with a NumPy reference, which reproduces scikit-image
  with the default box; flip equivariance in 2D and 3D; no effect in slow
  mode; tiled vs direct; kernel compilation in 2D–4D.

## Deviations from scikit-image

- **dtype:** 8/16-bit integer and bool inputs are processed and returned as
  float32 (table above).
- **Output shape:** always the input's shape. scikit-image calls `np.squeeze`,
  which also drops size-1 spatial axes.
- **Argument checks:** `ValueError` for negative `patch_size` or
  `patch_distance`, and for `h <= 0`. scikit-image returns NaN or garbage.
- **Slow-mode overflow:** in slow mode, a patch whose final distance exceeds
  708 gets zero weight. scikit-image skips the cutoff after the last patch row
  and evaluates `_fast_exp` outside its domain there, which gives huge negative
  weights that dominate the average. A test includes an image where
  scikit-image returns 0.02 for a row whose correct value is 0.

## Benchmarks

**Repo benchmark script** (`benchmarks/skimage/cucim_restoration_bench.py`):
noisy `camera` image, RTX A6000 vs scikit-image 0.26 on one core of an
i9-10980XE. 2D uses `patch_size=7, patch_distance=11`; 3D uses
`patch_size=5, patch_distance=5`; `h=0.04`.

| Shape | dtype | Mode | scikit-image | cuCIM | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256×256 | float32 | fast | 193 ms | 0.44 ms | 437× |
| 256×256 | float32 | slow | 4.87 s | 0.51 ms | 9,637× |
| 512×512 | float32 | fast | 736 ms | 1.38 ms | 531× |
| 512×512 | float32 | slow | 19.0 s | 1.61 ms | 11,760× |
| 512×512×3 (RGB) | float32 | fast | 928 ms | 1.88 ms | 495× |
| 512×512×3 (RGB) | float32 | slow | 23.9 s | 2.17 ms | 11,041× |
| 64×64×64 | float32 | fast | 4.68 s | 5.00 ms | 937× |
| 64×64×64 | float32 | slow | 67.6 s | 6.83 ms | 9,900× |
| 512×512 | uint8 | fast | 725 ms | 1.43 ms | 506× |
| 512×512 | uint8 | slow | 16.3 s | 1.64 ms | 9,955× |

**Precision and image size** (public API end to end; uniform random input,
`h=0.1`):

| Case | cuCIM float32 | cuCIM float64 | scikit-image |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2D 128², fast, s=7, d=11 | 0.24 ms | 1.1 ms | 33 ms |
| 2D 256², fast, s=7, d=11 | 0.47 ms | 3.8 ms | 102 ms |
| 2D 512², fast, s=7, d=11 | 1.40 ms | 16 ms | 380 ms |
| 2D 2048², fast, s=7, d=11 | 21 ms | 216 ms | — |
| 3D 32³, fast, s=5, d=5 | 0.68 ms | 5.5 ms | 582 ms |
| 3D 64³, fast, s=5, d=5 | 5.3 ms | 47 ms | 3.10 s |
| 3D 128³, fast, s=5, d=5 | 36 ms | 328 ms | — |

**Effect of the vendored `pad` and search-window splitting.** These are
end-to-end float32 timings, using `cupy.pad` without splitting ("Before") and
using both changes ("After"):

| Case | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2D 128², fast, s=7, d=11 | 0.44 ms | 0.24 ms | 1.8× |
| 2D 256², fast, s=7, d=11 | 0.73 ms | 0.47 ms | 1.6× |
| 2D 512², fast, s=7, d=11 | 1.61 ms | 1.40 ms | 1.15× |
| 3D 32³, fast, s=5, d=5 | 1.16 ms | 0.68 ms | 1.7× |

Splitting alone (measured with the same padding in both cases):

- 2D 256², s=7, d=11: 1.28× (fast) and 1.24× (slow).
- 3D 48³, s=5, d=5: 1.17×.
- 4D 16⁴, s=5, d=2: 1.34×.
- Configurations with little work per pixel are unchanged, e.g. 256² RGB with
  d=5, or the direct kernel.

## Tests

- **Ported:** all 13 scikit-image `denoise_nl_means` tests, in
  `restoration/tests/test_denoise.py`.
- **New `restoration/tests/test_non_local_means.py`:**
  - direct comparisons against scikit-image on the CPU: 2D, 3D, 4D; 1–12
    channels; fast and slow; σ = 0 and 0.1; odd and even patch sizes;
    `patch_distance` larger than the image; `channel_axis` 0, 1 and −1;
    non-contiguous input; uint8 input with both `preserve_range` settings;
  - the slow-mode early-exit and overflow cases;
  - the dtype matrix and `compute_dtype`;
  - shape preservation and argument validation;
  - tiled vs direct cross-checks, including non-default tiles and the fallback
    when shared memory is too small;
  - split vs unsplit search windows (2–100 chunks, both kernels, both modes);
  - images with size-1 spatial axes, against scikit-image (this checks the
    reflect padding of singleton axes);
  - device-side `fast_exp` against a NumPy re-implementation of scikit-image's
    `_fast_exp`.
- **Opt-in 64-bit indexing test**, `test_nl_means_64bit_indexing`:
  - Set `CUCIM_RUN_NL_MEANS_MEM_TEST=1` to run it (following the existing
    `CUCIM_RUN_TIFF_ITERATOR_MEM_TEST` convention). It also skips itself when
    less than 28 GB of GPU memory is free.
  - It denoises a 46341² float32 image (just over 2^31 elements) with
    `patch_distance=1`, which takes about 1 s and peaks at ~26 GB. It covers
    the tiled kernel in fast and slow mode and the direct kernel.
  - Each output pixel depends only on nearby input, so small crops processed
    with 32-bit indexing give the expected values. The crops include one
    straddling linear index 2^31 and one past it.
- **`test_denoise.py`:** `test_denoise_nl_means_slow_mode_4d_and_3d_multichannel`
  covers the cases scikit-image does not implement (slow mode, 3D multichannel
  and 4D): three identical channels give the grayscale 3D result exactly, and
  the 4D and 4D multichannel results are finite and raise the PSNR.
- The full restoration suite passes: 364 passed, 2 skipped (the opt-in test and
  one pre-existing skip). The opt-in test also passes when enabled.

### Validation beyond scikit-image

Slow mode for 3D multichannel and 4D images has no scikit-image result, so it
was checked in two other ways (scripts and results in the planning notes, not
part of the test suite):

- **Independent N-D reference.** A NumPy implementation written from the
  definition of slow mode (Gaussian patch taps, the early exit along the first
  axis, the clipped search window, `_fast_exp`) for any number of axes and
  channels. It equals scikit-image exactly (0.0) for 2D, 2D multichannel and
  3D. cuCIM equals it to 4e-16 (float64) in 10 cases: 3D multichannel (2 and 3
  channels), 4D and 4D multichannel, patch sizes 3 and 5, `sigma` 0 and 0.1.
  The comparison is sensitive: without the early exit the reference differs
  from cuCIM by 1e-2, and with an exact `exp` by 1e-3. The same reference shows
  that the small asymmetry of slow mode under a permutation of the axes (8e-3
  on a noisy 8^4 image) comes from the early exit being tested along the first
  axis only (1e-15 without it); fast mode has none and is symmetric (4e-16).
- **Synthetic denoising quality across dimensions.** A light n-ball (radius 10)
  in a 32^n cube with Gaussian noise (`sigma` = 0.25), `patch_size` 5 and
  `patch_distance` 3, with the PSNR measured on the central 2D slice so that
  every dimension is scored on the same disk (mean of 3 noise seeds). In slow
  mode (`h` = 0.6 sigma) the PSNR rises from 18.7 dB in 2D to 23.6 dB in 3D and
  28.0 dB in 4D, and 3D with 3 independent-noise channels gives 25.5 dB. In
  fast mode at `h` = 0.8 sigma it is 21.0, 22.4 and 21.0 dB: the best `h`
  falls as the patch has more elements, so at a fixed `h` the order is not
  guaranteed. With `h` tuned per dimension the best PSNR increases with the
  dimension in both modes (slow 21.2, 26.4, 28.8 dB; fast 20.9, 24.2, 24.8 dB
  in 2D, 3D, 4D). cuCIM equals scikit-image for 4D fast mode (2e-15 on a 14^4
  image), so the fast mode behaviour is that of the algorithm.

## Other changes

- `cucim_restoration_bench.py` and `run-nv-bench-restoration.sh` gain
  `denoise_nl_means` cases.
- `.pre-commit-config.yaml` registers the new scikit-image-derived modules
  with the `verify-copyright-skimage` hook, so they keep the
  `Apache-2.0 AND BSD-3-Clause` license identifier.
- **Bug fix:** `DenoiseBench` and `CalibratedDenoiseBench` added float64 noise
  to the image without casting back, so float32 benchmark requests actually ran
  in float64. This also affects the existing `denoise_tv_chambolle` and
  `calibrate_denoiser` benchmark results.

title: Add find_contours
body:
## Context

This MR builds upon the nanobind module that was introduced in #1197, so that MR should be reviewed first.

## Summary

This PR adds `cucim.skimage.measure.find_contours` for 2D CuPy arrays.
There was an issue requesting `active_contours` which is not implemented here,
but I think this is similar but not identical to OpenCV's findContours as
mentioned in this comment: https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/issues/483#issuecomment-1442477031.

The implementation follows scikit-image's marching-squares behavior: a GPU
RawKernel scans the 2D scalar field, identifies cells crossed by the requested
iso-value, resolves the marching-squares cases including the
`fully_connected` ambiguity, and emits line segments. The public API mirrors
`skimage.measure.find_contours`, including `level`, `fully_connected`,
`positive_orientation`, and `mask`. The contours come out in the same order and
with the same points as in scikit-image (the tests compare them exactly).

The keyword-only argument `output_kind` selects the form of the result and where
it lives:

| `output_kind` | Result | Arrays are |
|---|---|---|
| `"list"` (default) | a list with one array of shape `(n_points, 2)` per contour, matching scikit-image | NumPy (host) |
| `"packed"` | a tuple `(points, offsets)`; contour `i` is `points[offsets[i]:offsets[i + 1]]` | NumPy (host) |
| `"packed_device"` | the same tuple as `"packed"` | CuPy (GPU) |

With `"list"`, the arrays are views of a single array that holds the points of
all contours when the contours are assembled on the GPU (25,000 or more
segments, unambiguous links), and separate arrays otherwise; do not rely on
either. The packed kinds skip the creation of the per-contour arrays, which is
useful when there are many small contours (see Performance Notes), and
`"packed_device"` also skips the copy of the points to the host, which is the
better choice when the contours are used by device code. The docstring
recommends the packed kinds for performance; `"list"` is the default only for
compatibility with scikit-image.

## How the contours are assembled

Segment extraction is parallel over cells. Putting the segments in order into
contours is a graph problem, and where most of the time was spent in earlier
versions of this PR (the history of the branch shows the steps):

1. Every segment endpoint has an integer key that identifies the grid edge (or,
   when the level is exactly the value at a vertex, the vertex) it lies on, so
   segments are linked by comparing keys instead of floating point
   coordinates. This was first done by a C++ function (nanobind) with hash
   tables, in segment order, as scikit-image does it, and then with
   locality-preserving open-addressing tables.
2. The links are found on the GPU instead: the segments are matched to the
   segments that start where they end by sorting the start keys and searching
   the end keys. Segments of zero length are dropped.
3. The linked segments form open paths and closed loops. They are ranked on
   the GPU by list ranking with splitters: the
   paths are cut at the first segment of every open path, at about one segment
   in 64, and at one segment of each loop that got none of those, and one
   thread follows each sublist. The few sublists are arranged into
   contours on the host. This fixes the order of the contours (by lowest
   segment index, as in scikit-image), where each closed loop starts, and where
   every sublist goes. A last kernel writes the point that ends each segment
   into the packed array, which is the only thing copied back to the host
   (and not even that for `output_kind="packed_device"`).

When a key is the start or the end of more than one segment (this happens when
the level is exactly the value of a vertex, for example in integer images)
the links are ambiguous, and the sequential C++ assembler (which gives scikit-image's
result in that case) is used. It is also used for fewer than 25,000
segments, since the device assembly has a fixed cost of about 1 ms that a
small image does not repay. `find_contours` requires the compiled extension
`cucim.skimage._cucim_skimage_cpp_ext` and raises an `ImportError` if it is not
available (there is no pure-Python fallback).

## Performance Notes

float32 images, `level=0.0`, default options, on an RTX A6000 (CuPy 14.2.0)
against scikit-image 0.26.0 on an Intel i9-10980XE. The times are means of
calls over about 2 s (the GPU calls are synchronized), and the speedup over
scikit-image is in parentheses. The `circle` and `sine` fields have few
contours; `camera` is scikit-image's `camera` image, tiled, and has many small
contours. Images with at least 25,000 segments (the two `camera` rows of 2048x2048
and 4096x4096, and 4096x4096 `sine`) are linked and ordered on the GPU, and the
other rows on the host.

| Image | Segments | Contours | scikit-image (CPU) | cuCIM `"list"` | cuCIM `"packed"` | cuCIM `"packed_device"` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 512x512 circle | 1,368 | 1 | 3.1 ms | 0.22 ms (14x) | 0.22 ms (14x) | 0.31 ms (10x) |
| 512x512 sine | 5,660 | 13 | 7.6 ms | 0.41 ms (18x) | 0.40 ms (19x) | 0.48 ms (16x) |
| 512x512 camera | 20,143 | 1,869 | 24.1 ms | 3.20 ms (8x) | 1.89 ms (13x) | 2.02 ms (12x) |
| 2048x2048 circle | 5,496 | 1 | 41.5 ms | 0.65 ms (64x) | 0.64 ms (65x) | 0.69 ms (60x) |
| 2048x2048 sine | 22,699 | 13 | 62.4 ms | 1.50 ms (41x) | 1.50 ms (42x) | 1.62 ms (39x) |
| 2048x2048 camera | 328,585 | 29,544 | 625.8 ms | 13.3 ms (47x) | 5.08 ms (123x) | 4.46 ms (140x) |
| 4096x4096 circle | 10,992 | 1 | 149.1 ms | 1.79 ms (83x) | 1.78 ms (84x) | 1.88 ms (79x) |
| 4096x4096 sine | 45,419 | 13 | 193.7 ms | 2.90 ms (67x) | 2.83 ms (68x) | 2.71 ms (72x) |
| 4096x4096 camera | 1,318,545 | 117,936 | 2433.9 ms | 41.9 ms (58x) | 16.8 ms (145x) | 14.7 ms (166x) |

Over all sizes from 256x256 to 4096x4096 (15 images) the speedup is 5x to
83x for `"list"` and 5x to 145x for `"packed"`. With few contours the three kinds
take about the same time. With many small contours, creating the list of NumPy
arrays is most of the time (the 4096x4096 `camera` image has 118K contours), so
the packed kinds are much faster, and `"packed_device"` is the fastest when the
contours are assembled on the GPU because it also skips the copy of the points
to the host. For images that are assembled on the host (fewer than 25,000
segments), `"packed_device"` has to upload the result and is about 0.1 ms slower
than `"packed"`. For the 4096x4096 `camera` image:

- the GPU segment extraction takes 2.6 ms and linking the segments 1.8 ms;
- assembling the contours (including the linking and the copy to the host)
  takes 14 ms, and `output_kind="packed"` takes 17 ms in all;
- the list of 118K NumPy arrays takes 42 ms in all, so with many small contours
  most of the time of the default output is the creation of the arrays.

Earlier versions of this PR assembled the contours on the host: this took
about 130 ns per segment with `std::unordered_map` and 60 ns with flat hash
tables. For a 4096x4096 smooth random image with 1.9M segments `find_contours`
took 314 ms with `std::unordered_map`, 207 ms with flat hash tables, 68 ms when
the links were found on the GPU and walked on the host, and 15 ms with the
assembly on the GPU.

## Image size

The kernels index the pixels, the cells and the offsets of the segment
coordinates with a 32-bit integer when that cannot overflow (fewer than `2**31`
pixels, and fewer than `2**29` segments in the kernel that writes them) and
with a 64-bit integer otherwise; the kernels are compiled for either, so the
time of smaller images is unchanged (a `find_contours` call on a smooth 4096²
float64 image at level 0.5: 1.5 ms before and after). A 46,500² float64 image
(2.16 billion pixels; the image is 17.3 GB and the cell counts and their scan
8.7 GB each) was checked with a circle (one closed contour, radius error
below 1e-3); the previous code returned no contour for it. The segment ids of the
assembly are 32-bit, so more than `2**31 - 1` segments raise a `ValueError`. The
tests run the 64-bit kernels on small images (by lowering the limit) and compare
with the 32-bit kernels for both connectivities, with and without a mask, and for
the packed output and the assembly on the device.

## Reviewer Notes

- The marching-squares segment generation and, for 25,000 or more segments, the linking and ordering of the
  segments run on the GPU; the points are copied to the host in one transfer
  (unless `output_kind="packed_device"` is used, which leaves them on the GPU).
- The compiled assembler (nanobind, `python/nanobind/skimage/`) is required:
  `find_contours` raises an `ImportError` without it. The pure-Python assembler
  was removed from the module and lives in the tests as the reference. The
  extension is the one already built and checked in the wheel and conda
  builds for the intensity median. Besides the small-image and ambiguous-link
  paths, the device assembly needs it for the arrangement of the sublists
  (`plan_linked_contours`).
- The tests compare the device assembly with the sequential assembler
  point by point, on random smooth images, loops, long spiral contours and masked
  images, and check the host assembler (ambiguous links) and the error without
  the extension.

title: cuslide2: make `pip install cucim-cu13` work and add tests for this
body:
## Summary

closes #1211

With cuCIM installed from PyPI, the cuslide2 plugin (`ENABLE_CUSLIDE2=1`) does not work as the
README describes:

1. **libnvimgcodec is not found.** `CuImage(path)` raises `dlopen libnvimgcodec.so failed!` for
   every TIFF, although `nvidia-nvimgcodec-cu13` is installed. That wheel puts `libnvimgcodec.so.0`
   in `site-packages/nvidia/nvimgcodec/`. The plugin only calls `dlopen` with bare library names,
   and its RPATH (rewritten by `auditwheel` to `cucim_cu13.libs`) does not include that directory.
2. **nvJPEG2000 and nvTIFF are not installed.** cuCIM requires the nvImageCodec wheel without its
   optional extras. When nvImageCodec cannot load nvTIFF and nvJPEG2000 ("Failed to load nvtiff
   library!"), cuslide2 reads the wrong pyramid for every TIFF (extra levels for the macro,
   thumbnail and label images; tile sizes of `(0, 0)`), returns **all-zero regions without an
   error** for Aperio JPEG 2000 (compression 33003) and standard JPEG 2000 (34712) images, and
   raises an error for Aperio RGB JPEG 2000 (33005).
3. **The README and the test scripts** do not work with pip installs, and the scripts report success
   on zero-filled images.

Tested with `cucim-cu13==26.10.0` from PyPI in a fresh virtual environment (Python 3.13,
`nvidia-nvimgcodec-cu13==0.9.0.20`), and with the nightly `26.12.0a34` wheel, which behaves the same
way. With `nvidia-nvimgcodec-cu13[nvjpeg2k,nvtiff]` and the library directory on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`,
the same files are read correctly (the same pyramids, tile sizes and region means as the legacy
plugin).

## Changes

1. **Depend on the nvImageCodec extras** (`dependencies.yaml`, regenerated `pyproject.toml`):
   `nvidia-nvimgcodec-cu12/-cu13[nvjpeg,nvjpeg2k,nvtiff]>=0.9.0,<0.10.0`. Constraints files cannot
   contain extras, so they keep the plain requirement.
2. **Find libnvimgcodec in the pip package** (`nvimgcodec_wrap.cc`). The default search (system,
   conda, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`) is tried first, as before. If it fails, the plugin also tries
   `<directory of the plugin>/../../nvidia/nvimgcodec/`, which is where the pip package is relative
   to `site-packages/cucim/clara/`. The error message now lists every path that was tried and names
   the pip and conda packages. The warning about missing TIFF tags now mentions the nvTIFF and
   nvJPEG2000 libraries.
3. **Tests on synthetic images** (`python/cucim/tests/unit/clara/test_cuslide2_plugin.py`).
   Pyramidal, tiled RGB TIFF files are written with tifffile (Deflate, LZW, JPEG, JPEG 2000), so no
   sample data is downloaded. In a new process with `ENABLE_CUSLIDE2=1`, each test checks the level
   count, level dimensions and tile sizes, and that regions read on the CPU and on the GPU match the
   source image (exactly for the lossless codecs, within a small mean error for the lossy ones) and
   are not all zero. The tests are skipped only if the package has no cuslide2 plugin. If it has
   one, a missing nvImageCodec, nvTIFF or nvJPEG2000 library is a test failure.
4. **README and scripts.** The README lists the requirements for cuslide2 with pip.
   `scripts/test_common.py` used only the plugin directory of a source build (so the scripts failed
   with pip and conda installs); it now falls back to the installed package. The scripts now fail on
   tile sizes of `(0, 0)` (before: "skipping caching assertions") and on all-zero decoded tiles
   (before, GPU and CPU both returned zeros and matched).

## Testing

- The new tests pass (4 passed) against a source build with the nvImageCodec, nvJPEG2000, nvTIFF and
  nvJPEG libraries. With nvJPEG2000 and nvTIFF removed from the library path, they fail: no TIFF
  tags are returned, and `read_region` raises `Failed to decode IFD[0] with nvImageCodec`.
- The library lookup was checked on its own: `nvimgcodec_wrap.cc` was compiled with
  `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` into a shared object placed in a layout like `site-packages/cucim/clara/`
  next to `site-packages/nvidia/nvimgcodec/` (from the `nvidia-nvimgcodec-cu13` wheel), with no
  `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`. It loads the library through the new fallback, and with the `nvidia` directory
  removed it fails with the message that lists the paths.

## Not in this PR

- The plugin still returns zeros without an error for a JPEG 2000 file when a decoder is missing and
  nvImageCodec reports success after the per-tile failures. The extras remove the cause for pip
  installs; checking that a decoder is registered before decoding is left for a later change.
- cuslide2 cannot read strip-based JPEG associated images (the Philips TIFF macro image).

title: Build the wheel with a single copy of libcucim
body:
## Summary
closes #1213

The pip wheels load two copies of libcucim. After opening a file, `/proc/self/maps` lists both:

- `cucim/clara/_cucim*.so` needs `libcucim.so.26`, found next to it in `cucim/clara/`.
- The plugins (`cucim.kit.cuslide@*.so`, `cucim.kit.cuslide2@*.so`, `cucim.kit.cumed@*.so`) need
  `libcucim-<hash>.so.<version>` in `cucim_cu13.libs/`, a renamed copy that `auditwheel repair`
  vendored.

Each copy has its own global state, so the cache configured from Python is not the one the plugins
use. With a per-process cache and statistics recording on, a cold `read_region` records neither hits
nor misses, for both cuslide and cuslide2:

```python
CuImage.cache("per_process", memory_capacity=256)
CuImage.cache().record(True)
CuImage("slide.svs").read_region((0, 0), (512, 512), level=0)
print(CuImage.cache().hit_count, CuImage.cache().miss_count)   # wheels: 0 0
```

I saw this with `cucim-cu13==26.10.0` and the `26.12.0a34` nightly. The conda packages and a source
build load one copy and record misses. It also makes the caching step of
`scripts/test_aperio_svs.py` and `scripts/test_philips_tiff.py` fail with wheels.

## Cause

The wheel is assembled from the CMake build tree (`run build_local` copies
`build-release/lib*/cucim*` into `python/cucim/src/cucim/clara/`). In the build tree, the plugins'
RUNPATH is the absolute path of the libcucim build directory and has no `$ORIGIN`, because
`CMAKE_INSTALL_RPATH` (`$ORIGIN`) only applies to the installed copy. The Python extension finds
`libcucim.so.26` through `$ORIGIN`, so `auditwheel` sees it as part of the wheel. For the plugins it
resolves `libcucim.so.26` to the build directory, copies that file into `cucim_cu13.libs/` with a
hashed name, and rewrites the plugins' `NEEDED` entry to the new name.

## Changes

- Set `BUILD_WITH_INSTALL_RPATH` on the three plugin targets, so the plugins in the build tree have
  RPATH `$ORIGIN`, like the installed ones. `auditwheel` then finds the `libcucim.so.26` that is
  already in the wheel.
- `ci/validate_wheel.sh` fails if a wheel contains a vendored `*.libs/libcucim-*`.
- New unit test `test_libcucim_loaded_once.py`: after a read by a plugin, exactly one libcucim is
  mapped into the process, and the cache configured from Python has recorded the read. It uses a
  generated TIFF, so no download is needed.

## Testing

I reproduced the problem with `auditwheel` 6.8.2 on a wheel assembled from a local source build of
`main`:

| Plugins' RUNPATH in the wheel | `auditwheel repair` result |
|---|---|
| absolute build path (current) | adds `cucim.libs/libcucim-f2d0d9dd.so.26.12.00` |
| `$ORIGIN` (the new RPATH) | adds nothing; one `libcucim.so.26` in the wheel |

The second row was made with `patchelf --set-rpath '$ORIGIN'` on the plugins, which is what the
CMake property does to the files in the build tree. I did not rebuild the plugins with the changed
CMake files and then make a wheel. The new check in `validate_wheel.sh` flags the first wheel and
accepts the second. The new unit test passes with a source build.

CI builds the wheels, so the wheel build, `validate_wheel.sh` and the wheel tests are the final
check.

title: conda: build and package the cuslide2 plugin in libcucim
body:
**This PR is on top of #1219** (https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/pull/1219), so that the tests
added there (`test_cuslide2_plugin.py`, synthetic TIFF files written with tifffile) also run against
the conda packages. Until #1219 is merged, this PR also shows its two commits. The change here is
the last commit, `conda: build and package the cuslide2 plugin in libcucim`.

## Summary

closes #1212

The `libcucim` conda package does not contain `cucim.kit.cuslide2@<version>.so`. With
`ENABLE_CUSLIDE2=1`, opening any TIFF fails:

```text
[Plugin: cucim.kit.cuslide2] Could not load the dynamic library from cucim.kit.cuslide2@26.10.00.so. ...
RuntimeError: Dependent library 'cucim.kit.cuslide2@26.10.00.so' cannot be loaded!
```

The recipe builds only the other two plugins (`for plugin_name in cuslide cumed`). The pip wheels
ship cuslide2, and the recipe already depends on `libnvimgcodec` (which brings in `libnvjpeg`,
`libnvjpeg2k0` and `libnvtiff`), but nothing in the package used it. I saw this with the `26.10.00`
packages from the rapidsai channel and with the `26.12.00a34` nightly `libcucim`.

## Changes

- `conda/recipes/libcucim/recipe.yaml`: build `cuslide2` together with `cuslide` and `cumed`. The
  static helper library of cuslide2 (`libnvimgcodec_dynlink.a`, only needed to link the plugin) is
  removed from the package.
- `README.md`: the notice in the cuslide2 section said that `cuslide` is deprecated from 26.04 and
  removed in 26.08. It now says that `cuslide` is still the default plugin, that `cuslide2` is
  opt-in and is included in the pip wheels and in the conda packages, and that `cuslide` is planned
  to be deprecated. Please check the wording of the deprecation plan.

nvImageCodec is loaded at runtime with `dlopen`. The plugin's RPATH is `$ORIGIN`, so it finds
`$PREFIX/lib/libnvimgcodec.so.0` and `$PREFIX/lib/extensions/` from the `libnvimgcodec` dependency.
The pip-specific changes (extras, library lookup in `site-packages/nvidia/nvimgcodec`) are in #1219
and are not needed here.

## Testing

I built the recipe locally with `rattler-build` 0.80.0 (`--experimental`, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.13,
channels rapidsai and conda-forge, without sccache), following `ci/build_cpp.sh`:

- The build succeeds, including the overlinking check. The package contains `cucim.kit.cuslide@`,
  `cucim.kit.cuslide2@` and `cucim.kit.cumed@26.12.00.so` in `lib/`, each with RPATH `$ORIGIN/`, and
  no `libnvimgcodec_dynlink.a`.
- I installed the package into a new environment with `mamba` (this pulled in `libnvimgcodec` 0.9.0,
  `libnvjpeg2k0`, `libnvtiff` and `libnvjpeg`), and ran the tests from #1219 with the plugin
  directory of the Python package set to that environment's `lib` and no `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`: 4 passed
  (Deflate, LZW, JPEG and JPEG 2000 pyramids, on the CPU and the GPU).
- The Python extension in that run came from a source build of `main` because I did not build the
  `cucim` conda package. Only the plugins came from the conda package.

CI builds and tests the packages, so it is the final check. In particular, the tests from #1219 now
run with the plugin in the conda test jobs.

## Not in this PR

- The wheels load two copies of libcucim (separate PR).
- cuslide2 cannot read strip-based JPEG associated images (the Philips TIFF macro image).
