title: cuslide2: raise an error instead of returning zeros when no JPEG 2000 decoder is loaded
body:
The issue fixed was discovered along with #1211 and described there, but was not the main focus of that issue.

**This PR is on top of #1219** (https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim/pull/1219), which adds the
synthetic-image tests that this PR extends. Until #1219 is merged, this PR also shows its two
commits. The change here is the last commit.

## Summary

If the nvJPEG2000 or nvTIFF library cannot be loaded, `read_region` on a JPEG 2000 TIFF (Aperio
compression 33003 and 33005, or TIFF compression 34712) returns an **all-zero image without an
error**, on the CPU and on the GPU. nvImageCodec prints `Failed to load nvjpeg2k library!` or
`Failed to load nvtiff library!` once, and OpenCV prints
`Compression scheme 33003 tile decoding is not implemented` for each tile, but the call returns
normally. The caller cannot tell the image from a black one.

Cause: nvImageCodec has CPU-only fallback decoders for TIFF (libtiff and OpenCV extensions). They
accept a JPEG 2000 TIFF, fail on every tile, and report success. cuslide2 checks the processing
status of the decode, but the status is success.

#1219 adds the nvImageCodec extras to the pip requirements, which removes the usual cause for pip
installs. This PR makes the failure visible when the libraries are missing anyway (a pip install
without the extras, a conda environment without `libnvjpeg2k` or `libnvtiff`, or a system install).

## Changes

- `NvImageCodecTiffParserManager::get_decoder_for(codec, compression_known)` returns the default
  decoder, except for JPEG 2000 IFDs, and for IFDs whose compression is not known because no TIFF
  tags were returned (nvTIFF is not loaded, so the compression cannot be ruled out). For those it
  returns a second decoder, created on first use, that allows only the GPU-only, hybrid CPU/GPU and
  hardware backends and not the CPU-only ones. If nvJPEG2000 or nvTIFF is missing, nvImageCodec then
  reports that the image cannot be decoded, and the existing error path raises.
- The three decode functions (single ROI, batch, async batch) get their decoder from
  `get_decoder_for`.
- The "Failed to decode IFD" error now names the missing libraries and the pip and conda packages.
- With no GPU (the CPU-only mode of the plugin) or when the restricted decoder cannot be created,
  the default decoder is used as before.
- Test: `test_cuslide2_jpeg2000_is_decoded_or_an_error` writes a JPEG 2000 TIFF with tifffile
  (33003, 33005 and 34712). A read must either match the source image (mean absolute error of at
  most 1) or raise an error that mentions nvImageCodec, and must never return blank data. No sample
  data is downloaded.

## Behavior change

Without nvTIFF, every compression now raises. Before, JPEG, Deflate and LZW TIFFs were decoded
correctly by the CPU fallbacks, but with a wrong pyramid (extra levels for the macro, thumbnail and
label images) and tile sizes of `(0, 0)`, so the image was not usable as a slide anyway. A pip
install with the extras from #1219 is not affected. Only a setup without nvTIFF is. If you prefer,
this can be limited to IFDs that are known to be JPEG 2000 (the second case in `get_decoder_for`),
which keeps the old behavior without nvTIFF but leaves the all-zero result in that setup.

## Testing

I built the plugin from this branch against a source build of libcucim and ran the new test with
three nvImageCodec layouts, with the old plugin (before this change) and the new one:

| nvImageCodec layout | old plugin | new plugin |
|---|---|---|
| pip package, no extras | 3 failed: blank region | 3 passed: error raised |
| pip package plus nvTIFF only | 3 failed: blank region | 3 passed: error raised |
| all libraries | 3 passed | 3 passed |

With all libraries, the 7 tests of `test_cuslide2_plugin.py` pass (the pyramids and pixels of
Deflate, LZW, JPEG and JPEG 2000 TIFFs on the CPU and the GPU). With the pip layout without extras,
the pyramid tests now fail with the new error instead of reading a wrong pyramid.

The `libnvimgcodec` libraries in these layouts are not loaded the same way in every environment, so
I did not add a test that removes them. The new test is a regression check that is useful when run
where a library is missing, and it passes where all libraries are present, as in CI.

title: Update cuslide2 to nvImageCodec 0.10.0
body:
Moves cuslide2 from nvImageCodec 0.9 to [v0.10.0](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvImageCodec/releases/tag/v0.10.0).

## Why this is not just a pin bump

cuslide2 `dlopen`s nvImageCodec (`WITH_DYNAMIC_NVIMGCODEC=ON` by default) and compiles against a vendored copy of the headers, so the headers have to move with the pin.

0.10 grew `nvimgcodecExecutionParams_t` by two plugin-selection fields, and the library now **rejects an execution-parameter `struct_size` that does not match its own header** with `NVIMGCODEC_STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR`. Compiling both vendored headers confirms the size change:

```
0.10.0 vendored: NVIMGCODEC_VER=1000 sizeof(ExecutionParams)=96
0.9.0  vendored: NVIMGCODEC_VER=900  sizeof(ExecutionParams)=80
```

`NvImageCodecTiffParserManager` sets `exec_params.struct_size = sizeof(nvimgcodecExecutionParams_t)`, so with the 0.9 headers against a 0.10 library every `nvimgcodecDecoderCreate` would fail. The pin and the vendored headers have to move together in one change.

## Changes

**Vendored headers.** `nvimgcodec.h` and `nvimgcodec_version.h` re-vendored from upstream `v0.10.0`. The in-tree 0.9 copy is upstream's verbatim apart from the short SPDX header and stripped trailing whitespace; applying that same transform to upstream v0.9.0 reproduces the committed file byte for byte, and the 0.10.0 copy here is produced the same way, so the diff is upstream's and nothing else.

**Version macro.** 0.10 replaces `MAKE_SEMANTIC_VERSION` with `NVIMGCODEC_MAKE_SEMANTIC_VERSION`, packing `major * 10000 + minor * 100 + patch` so a two-digit minor no longer overflows into the major. Updated at the two use sites and in the tests.

**Runtime gate** (`check_nvimgcodec_runtime_version`). Supported range moved to `>=0.10.0,<0.11.0`. The version it compares is produced by the *loaded* library, so an older library still reports the narrow encoding — but every released 0.x packs identically under both, so an old library is rejected on its version rather than misread as something in range. There is a test pinning that.

`format_nvimgcodec_version()` loses its ambiguous-value branch: it existed only because 0.10.0 and 1.0.0 both packed to 1000, which the widened encoding fixes, so diagnostics can now always name an exact version.

**Build-time gate** (`cmake/deps/nvimgcodec.cmake`). SONAME candidate `libnvimgcodec.so.0.9.0` → `libnvimgcodec.so.0.10.0` (upstream still builds `SOVERSION 0`, `VERSION 0.10.0`, so the `.so.0` and `.so` fallbacks are unchanged). Header and `find_package` checks moved to the 0.10 range, and the fatal-error text now names the actual incompatibility instead of asserting a general lack of backward compatibility.

**Packaging pins** → `>=0.10.0,<0.11.0` in `dependencies.yaml`, the four generated conda environments, `conda/recipes/libcucim/conda_build_config.yaml`, and `python/cucim/pyproject.toml`. All four packages are published at 0.10: `libnvimgcodec`, `libnvimgcodec-dev` and `nvimgcodec` at 0.10.0 on conda-forge, and `nvidia-nvimgcodec-cu12` / `-cu13` at 0.10.0.9 on PyPI.

## What did not need to change

- **Dynlink stubs.** All 21 nvImageCodec entry points cuslide2 resolves have byte-identical declarations in 0.9 and 0.10 (checked by parsing both headers), so `nvimgcodec_stubs_generated.cc` is unchanged. It compiles clean against the new header.
- **Symbol visibility.** 0.10 stops exporting internal C++ symbols from `libnvimgcodec.so`. The only symbol cuslide2 passes to `dlsym` is `nvimgcodecGetProperties`, a documented C API entry point.
- **Enum values.** The additions in 0.10 (`NVIMGCODEC_STRUCTURE_TYPE_PLUGIN_SELECTION`, `NVIMGCODEC_STATUS_RESOURCE_IN_USE = 22`, `NVIMGCODEC_BACKEND_KIND_ANY = 0`) are appended or explicitly numbered; nothing cuslide2 uses was renumbered.
- **Plugin selection.** `exec_params` is value-initialized, so the two new fields default to "no selection", which is the behavior cuslide2 wants.
- **Other structs.** `nvimgcodecImageInfo_t`, `nvimgcodecDecodeParams_t`, `nvimgcodecRegion_t`, `nvimgcodecCodeStreamView_t`, `nvimgcodecProperties_t`, `nvimgcodecInstanceCreateInfo_t`, `nvimgcodecMetadata_t`, `nvimgcodecCodeStreamInfo_t`, `nvimgcodecBackend_t` and `nvimgcodecBackendParams_t` are all unchanged.

## Testing

`test_nvimgcodec_version.cpp` was rewritten around the new range and encoding, including a case pinning that the narrow and widened encodings agree on released 0.x versions, which is what makes the runtime check sound across the transition.

Verified locally without a CUDA build:

- The 0.10.0 vendored header, `nvimgcodec_stubs_generated.cc` and `nvimgcodec_wrap.cc` all compile against the new headers.
- `nvimgcodec_wrap.cc`'s SONAME macros now produce the dlopen order `libnvimgcodec.so.0.10.0`, `libnvimgcodec.so.0`, `libnvimgcodec.so`.
- Every assertion in the rewritten test file passes when the gate functions are compiled standalone against the new version header.

A GPU run against a real 0.10 install is still needed; that is what CI covers.

Fixes #1204
Fixes #1195

title: Faster GPU thresholding: histogram thresholds, Otsu, multi-Otsu, etc.
body:
## Description

This PR speeds up the functions of `cucim.skimage.filters.thresholding` that
were limited by host code, by passes over the image, or by the amount of work of
the algorithm, and adds an exact GPU search to `threshold_multiotsu`. No
function changes its signature or what it returns (a scalar threshold, an array
of thresholds, or a threshold image, as in scikit-image).

- **`threshold_otsu`, `threshold_yen`, `threshold_isodata`,
  `threshold_triangle`** run in GPU kernels on the histogram instead of copying
  it to the host. One block of 512 threads handles any number of bins: each
  thread owns a chunk of consecutive bins, the chunk sums are scanned in shared
  memory, every thread evaluates the criterion for its bins and the first
  maximum is kept. The histogram-based functions skip the pass over the image
  that checked for a constant image (the histogram shows it).
- **`exposure.histogram`** computes the histogram of `uint8` and `int8` images
  in one pass (per-warp histograms in shared memory), without the passes that
  find the minimum and the maximum.
- **`threshold_multiotsu`** finds the thresholds with an exact dynamic
  programming search on the GPU, in float64. Each stage is searched by divide
  and conquer, `O(classes * nbins * log(nbins))` instead of the exhaustive
  `O(nbins**(classes - 1))` (or `O(classes * nbins**2)` for the plain dynamic
  programming).
- **`threshold_minimum`** runs the histogram smoothing loop (hundreds of
  iterations) in one kernel, without synchronizing with the host.
- **`threshold_li`** computes the threshold of integer images from the histogram
  (the default initial guess).
- **`threshold_niblack`, `threshold_sauvola`** compute the local mean and
  standard deviation with separable box sums instead of two float64 integral
  images.

## References

The multi-Otsu search is the dynamic programming ("shortest path") algorithm for
criteria that are sums of per-class costs, described by Luessi et al. (ICIP
2006, doi:10.1109/ICIP.2006.312426), who attribute it to Otsu for his method. It
maximizes the criterion of Liao et al. (2001), `S^2 / P` summed over the
classes, which is equivalent to Otsu's between-class variance (Otsu 1979,
doi:10.1109/TSMC.1979.4310076). The docstrings of `threshold_multiotsu` and
`threshold_otsu` cite these. The float64 accumulation, the GPU parallelization
over the end bin and the tie rule are specific to this implementation. Luessi et
al. also describe faster searches for large histograms that use the monotonicity
of the stage matrices: divide and conquer, `O(classes * nbins * log(nbins))`,
and SMAWK, `O(classes * nbins)`. The last commit uses divide and conquer (the
proof of the monotonicity is not in that paper, so it is tested: the thresholds
equal those of the plain search in all the cases tried, including exact ties).
SMAWK is not used: it is sequential and irregular.

## Differences from scikit-image

Most results are identical. The differences below come from defects or accuracy
limits of scikit-image, and each has a test.

- **`threshold_multiotsu`.** The kernels return the thresholds that maximize the
  variance between classes (among exactly equal maxima, the smallest in
  lexicographic order, as scikit-image does). scikit-image's search accumulates
  in float32 and gives the first bin a weight of one instead of zero in the
  class that contains it (`first_moment[0] = prob[0]` in `_multiotsu.pyx`), so
  for some histograms its result is not the maximum of the criterion. On the
  sample images of `skimage.data` that load offline the results are the same in
  54 of 57 cases (2 to 4 classes) and differ by one bin in the other 3. Against
  an exhaustive float64 search, 599 of 600 random histograms are identical (the
  other is an exact tie broken by rounding), and scikit-image's answer was never
  better than ours when evaluated with exact arithmetic on 900 random histograms
  (34 strictly worse, 39 exact ties). The docstring Notes say so.
- **Histograms of thousands of bins (16-bit images).** The kernels accumulate in
  float64, scikit-image in float32, so the thresholds can differ by a few bins
  where the criterion is flat near its maximum. For the 16-bit case in the tests
  the value of the criterion at our threshold is larger by a relative 6.6e-9.
- **`threshold_li`, signed integer images.** scikit-image subtracts the minimum
  in the image dtype, which overflows when the range is larger than the maximum
  of the type (`int8`: NaN or a wrong value). The result here equals
  scikit-image's for a float64 copy of the image.
- **`threshold_niblack`, `threshold_sauvola`.** The local standard deviation is
  computed in float64 before the result is cast. scikit-image casts the mean to
  float32 first, which loses the standard deviation of images with a large
  offset (for a float32 image with an offset of 1000 its error is 1.0 to 1.4
  times the maximum standard deviation, ours 2e-7 to 3e-7 of it). For
  integer-valued images the sums are exact, so ties (a pixel equal to the
  threshold) are the same as before.

## Benchmarks

4096 x 4096 images made from the scikit-image `camera` picture (`uint8`;
`uint16` and `float32` scaled to the range of the type). RTX A6000, CuPy 14.2.0,
scikit-image on an Intel i9-10980XE. GPU times are wall times with a
synchronization, the mean of the calls in about 1 s (at least 3; a single call
if it takes longer). "GPU before" is `upstream/main` (the host implementations)
and "GPU after" this branch. The scikit-image times are for the whole function
on a NumPy array, including its histogram.

### Histogram-based global thresholds

| Function | Image | scikit-image (CPU) | GPU before | GPU after | after vs before | after vs scikit-image |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `threshold_otsu` | uint8 | 55.6 ms | 1.17 ms | 0.31 ms | 3.8x | 182x |
| `threshold_otsu` | uint16 | 69.6 ms | 2.95 ms | 2.01 ms | 1.5x | 34.6x |
| `threshold_otsu` | float32 | 148 ms | 1.39 ms | 1.09 ms | 1.3x | 136x |
| `threshold_yen` | uint8 | 50.7 ms | 0.85 ms | 0.28 ms | 3.1x | 182x |
| `threshold_yen` | uint16 | 63.0 ms | 2.36 ms | 1.78 ms | 1.3x | 35.4x |
| `threshold_yen` | float32 | 143 ms | 1.22 ms | 1.05 ms | 1.2x | 136x |
| `threshold_isodata` | uint8 | 51.9 ms | 1.02 ms | 0.27 ms | 3.8x | 195x |
| `threshold_isodata` | uint16 | 63.0 ms | 2.44 ms | 1.97 ms | 1.2x | 32.0x |
| `threshold_isodata` | float32 | 142 ms | 1.23 ms | 1.04 ms | 1.2x | 137x |
| `threshold_triangle` | uint8 | 50.4 ms | 0.81 ms | 0.28 ms | 2.9x | 182x |
| `threshold_triangle` | uint16 | 64.3 ms | 1.99 ms | 1.42 ms | 1.4x | 45.4x |
| `threshold_triangle` | float32 | 143 ms | 1.18 ms | 1.10 ms | 1.1x | 130x |

For `uint8` images the time is now dominated by launches and one transfer. For
16-bit images, the histogram (`cupy.bincount` of 65,536 bins, about 1.3 ms) is
most of the time.

### Other functions

| Function | Image | scikit-image (CPU) | GPU before | GPU after | after vs before | after vs scikit-image |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `threshold_minimum` | uint8 | 87.6 ms | 31.3 ms | 7.51 ms | 4.2x | 11.7x |
| `threshold_li` | uint8 | 103 ms | 5.16 ms | 0.46 ms | 11.2x | 223x |
| `threshold_li` | uint16 | 123 ms | 7.99 ms | 4.37 ms | 1.8x | 28.2x |
| `threshold_niblack` | uint8 window 15 | 840 ms | 21.0 ms | 6.41 ms | 3.3x | 131x |
| `threshold_niblack` | float32 window 15 | 779 ms | 21.2 ms | 6.38 ms | 3.3x | 122x |
| `threshold_sauvola` | uint8 window 15 | 847 ms | 22.0 ms | 6.89 ms | 3.2x | 123x |
| `threshold_sauvola` | float32 window 15 | 812 ms | 21.8 ms | 6.98 ms | 3.1x | 116x |
| `exposure.histogram` | uint8 | 50.3 ms | 0.69 ms | 0.23 ms | 3.0x | 220x |

### `threshold_multiotsu` (256 bins)

| Function | Image | scikit-image (CPU) | GPU before | GPU after | after vs before | after vs scikit-image |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `threshold_multiotsu` | uint8 2 classes | 50.3 ms | 0.86 ms | 0.41 ms | 2.1x | 123x |
| `threshold_multiotsu` | uint8 3 classes | 50.9 ms | 1.53 ms | 0.46 ms | 3.4x | 112x |
| `threshold_multiotsu` | uint8 4 classes | 87.1 ms | 40.7 ms | 0.53 ms | 76x | 163x |
| `threshold_multiotsu` | uint8 5 classes | 2.55 s | 2.61 s | 0.62 ms | 4,230x | 4,133x |
| `threshold_multiotsu` | uint8 6 classes | n/a | 136 s | 0.68 ms | 199,000x | n/a |

scikit-image times are shown up to 5 classes. The "before" times for 5 and 6
classes are the scikit-image search on the host (6 classes took 136 s). For a
16-bit image (65,536 bins, the 4096 x 4096 `uint16` image above) the search
takes 2.1 ms for 2 classes (most of it the histogram), 4.2 ms for 3 classes, 6.3
ms for 4 classes, 7.9 ms for 5 classes and 9.2 ms for 6 classes. Before the last
commit (the plain dynamic programming, `O(classes * nbins**2)`) it took 0.17 s
for 3 classes and 0.33 s for 4 classes.

## Tests

- `test_thresholding.py`: block kernels against scikit-image for 8-bit and
  16-bit images (with the tolerance explained above); multi-Otsu against an
  exhaustive float64 search, for a 16-bit image and for the error cases, and
  against a plain `O(nbins**2)` dynamic programming for random, tie-heavy,
  sparse and palindromic histograms (divide and conquer); constant images (value
  and dtype); `threshold_minimum` against scikit-image on synthetic histograms
  (values and errors, 16 to 4200 bins); `threshold_li` for `uint8`, `uint16`,
  `int16` and `int8` images, with the iteration callback; the local statistics
  of Niblack and Sauvola against a float64 reference for an image with a large
  offset.
- `test_exposure.py`: the one-pass histogram for `uint8` and `int8`, both
  `source_range` values, constant, narrow and two-valued images, and an
  unaligned view.
- The tests of the `filters` and `exposure` modules pass (6946 passed, 25
  skipped).

title: regionprops: shape enhancements (surface_area, perimeter_convex, oriented bbox)
body:
## Context

This PR is the sixth in a stack of regionprops PRs. It builds on the regionprops bug fixes in #1196,
the performance improvements in #1198, the faster filled-region properties in #1208, the batch
convex-hull PR #1209 and the GPU 3D convex hull PR #1210, in that order; the last two have no PR
numbers yet. Please review and merge those first; until they merge, this PR's diff also contains
their commits, so review only the commits listed under "Commits" below.

**Caveat on correctness.** I am not an expert in convex-hull or computational-geometry algorithms
(the rotating calipers, the oriented and minimum-area bounding boxes) or in integral-geometry
estimators (the Crofton surface area), and the implementation was written with an AI agent. I have
not proven it correct; I verified it empirically, against SimpleITK, DIPlib, brute-force
computations and closed forms. This is how much confidence the tests support:

- *Well supported:* where ITK or DIPlib define the same quantity, the values agree: `surface_area`
  with SimpleITK's 3D `Perimeter` to 9e-14 for isotropic spacing, the oriented box with SimpleITK's
  to 4e-13, `perimeter_convex` with DIPlib's `ConvexPerimeter` to 4e-16, and DIPlib's maximum Feret
  diameter and its angle (up to ties). The minimum Feret diameter, its perpendicular width and the
  angles equal a brute-force computation on the same polygon on 42 blob regions and 5 hand-made
  shapes. Axis-aligned boxes are checked against closed forms.
- *In CI:* only the closed-form and brute-force checks and smaller fixed cases run
  (`test_surface_area*`, `test_feret_calipers_2d`, `test_oriented_bbox*`, listed under "Testing").
  The comparisons with SimpleITK and DIPlib were run by hand in a separate environment
  (`regionprops-perf/shape_extras_check.py`: not committed), because those libraries are not test
  dependencies.
- *Weaker, by design:* these are estimators, not exact quantities. `surface_area` is not exact and
  its error does not shrink with the resolution (see the docstring: up to 7.3% too small for faces
  normal to an axis); with anisotropic spacing it deliberately differs from ITK's by up to 26%
  because the direction weights are recomputed for the spacing, and that choice is checked only
  against exact ellipsoid areas, not against a reference implementation. The oriented box is not the
  smallest box, and is arbitrary when principal moments are equal.
- *No oracle:* for DIPlib's minimum Feret width, which is wrong on 2 of the 42 blobs (see
  "Agreement"), the comparison is with brute force, not DIPlib.

This PR adds cuCIM-only shape properties to the batch region properties
(`regionprops_table(..., batch_processing=True)` / `regionprops_dict`). Most are adopted from ITK
and DIPlib; the minimum-area rectangle is the quantity of OpenCV's `cv2.minAreaRect`. They
complement existing functionality well, but scikit-image has none of them:

- `surface_area` (3D);
- `feret_diameter_min`, `feret_diameter_min_perpendicular`, `feret_angle_max` and `feret_angle_min`
  (2D);
- `perimeter_convex` (2D);
- `oriented_bbox_size` and `oriented_bbox_center` (2D and 3D);
- `oriented_bbox_corners`, a public function that returns the corners of the oriented boxes;
- `min_area_bbox_size`, `min_area_bbox_center`, `min_area_bbox_angle` and `min_area_bbox_corners`
  (the minimum-area enclosing rectangle, 2D only).

The oriented bounding box relies on two fixes from the bug-fix PR #1196, found while writing this
one: `inertia_tensor_eigenvectors` (commit 23; the vectors it returned were not eigenvectors) and
the double-precision atomic minimum and maximum (commit 22).

The ideas for the other properties come from reading ITK's and DIPlib's implementations. The
minimum-area rectangle follows the rotating-calipers method (Freeman and Shapira 1975); I did not
read OpenCV's implementation or compare its results.

## Summary

| # | Commit | Properties | Checked against |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add a batch surface_area for 3D regions | `surface_area` | SimpleITK `Perimeter` (3D): 9e-14 |
| 2 | Add the minimum Feret diameter and Feret angles in 2D | `feret_diameter_min`, `feret_diameter_min_perpendicular`, `feret_angle_max`, `feret_angle_min` | brute force: exact; DIPlib `Feret` |
| 3 | Add the perimeter of the convex hull in 2D | `perimeter_convex` | DIPlib `ConvexPerimeter`: 4e-16 |
| 4 | Add the oriented bounding box | `oriented_bbox_size`, `oriented_bbox_center` (2D, 3D) | SimpleITK oriented bounding box: 4e-13 |
| 5 | Compute the surface_area weights for the voxel spacing | (`surface_area` with anisotropic spacing) | closed-form counts for boxes: 1e-12 |
| 6 | Document that the oriented box is not the smallest box | (docstrings only) | |
| 7 | Cache the surface_area coefficients for each spacing | (`surface_area` speed: 1.3–4.0×) | values unchanged |
| 8 | Add oriented_bbox_corners | `oriented_bbox_corners` (public function of the properties' dict or table) | formula against an explicit loop, enclosing every pixel |
| 9 | Add the minimum-area enclosing rectangle of 2D regions | `min_area_bbox_size`, `min_area_bbox_center`, `min_area_bbox_angle` (2D), `min_area_bbox_corners` | brute force over the hull edges: 1e-10 |

Main results (details in the sections below):

- **Values.**
  - `surface_area` equals SimpleITK's 3D `Perimeter` to 9e-14 for isotropic spacing.
  - The oriented box equals SimpleITK's to 4e-13 wherever the principal moments are distinct.
  - The five Feret values equal a brute-force computation.
  - `perimeter_convex` equals DIPlib's `ConvexPerimeter` to 4e-16 on the same polygon.
- **Deliberate differences from ITK.**
  - For anisotropic spacing, `surface_area` recomputes its direction weights. This narrows the error
    range for flat faces from −24.5%…+25% to −12.6%…+9.4% at spacing (2, 1, 1).
  - The oriented box is reported as its size and center, which do not depend on the eigenvector
    signs. ITK reports a corner, which does.
- **Speed against scikit-image** (closest equivalents, which compute less or something else, one CPU
  thread):
  - the six Feret and convex-perimeter values: 295–6000× faster than scikit-image's
    `feret_diameter_max` alone;
  - the oriented box: 86–3500×;
  - `surface_area`: 310–3700× faster than marching cubes per region.
- **Speed against SimpleITK and DIPlib** (20 CPU threads):
  - SimpleITK: 8–154×;
  - DIPlib's `Feret` and `ConvexPerimeter`: 18–80×;
  - DIPlib's `SurfaceArea` (another estimator): 520–680×.
- **Cost.** Each new property group takes 0.2–1.7 ms on an RTX A6000, for 8 to 16 256 labels.

Every region is measured as if it were alone in the image, like the other batch properties. The
`regionprops_dict` docstring gets a Notes section. It lists all cuCIM-only properties, how to
compute the oriented box's corners, and the known accuracy limits.

## What is added

- **surface_area (3D).** The discrete Crofton estimate over the 13 directions to the neighbors of a
  voxel, as ITK's `ShapeLabelMapFilter` computes the `Perimeter` of 3D objects (Lehmann and Legland,
  Insight Journal 2012).
  - **Formula.** Each voxel of a region checks its 26 neighbors. For every neighbor that has another
    label or lies outside the image, it adds `2 · c · V / |d|`. Here `c` is the area of that
    direction's Voronoi cell on the unit sphere, as a fraction of the sphere for the direction and
    its opposite. `V` is the voxel volume and `|d|` the spacing-scaled step.
  - **Isotropic weights.** These are ITK's constants: 0.0915558 for an axis, 0.0739613 for a face
    diagonal and 0.0703913 for a body diagonal. They were computed independently with
    `scipy.spatial.SphericalVoronoi`, and a test does so too.
  - **Anisotropic weights.** Unlike ITK, cuCIM recomputes them as the Voronoi cells of the
    spacing-scaled directions (commit 5), as Lang, Ohser and Hilfer (J. Microsc. 2001) propose.
  - **Accuracy.** The estimate is not exact, and its error does not shrink as the resolution grows
    (Ziegel and Kiderlen, 2010).
    - Balls of radius 20 voxels or more are within 0.5%.
    - A flat face is measured times a factor that depends on its orientation: 0.927 (faces normal to
      an axis) to 1.023 with isotropic spacing.
    - An axis-aligned cube of side 120 voxels is 7.8% too small.
- **feret_diameter_min, feret_diameter_min_perpendicular (2D).** The smallest caliper width of the
  region, and the caliper width perpendicular to its direction, as DIPlib's `Feret` (`Min` and
  `PerpMin`).
- **feret_angle_max, feret_angle_min (2D).** The directions of the maximum and minimum Feret
  diameters, as DIPlib's `MaxAng` and `MinAng`, but in the convention of `orientation`. That is the
  angle of the direction (d0, d1) from axis 0 towards axis 1, `atan2(d1, d0)`, folded into (−π/2,
  π/2]. DIPlib's angles, in its (x, y) coordinates, are π/2 minus these. With ties (several equally
  long diameters, or equally narrow directions), one of them is returned.
- **perimeter_convex (2D).** The length of the convex hull polygon, as DIPlib's `ConvexPerimeter`.
- **oriented_bbox_size, oriented_bbox_center (2D, 3D).** The bounding box aligned with the principal
  axes (the columns `V[:, a]` of `inertia_tensor_eigenvectors`) that encloses all the region's
  pixels, as ITK's oriented bounding box.
  - The size is the box's extent along each axis, in the order of the eigenvectors (the first is the
    shortest axis, as in ITK).
  - The center is in the coordinates of `centroid`.
  - The corners are `center + Σ_a ±size[a]/2 · V[:, a]`.
  - The box is not the smallest enclosing box: for a right triangle with legs of 200 and 100 pixels
    it is 6% larger than the smallest rectangle. When principal moments are equal it is arbitrary.
- **oriented_bbox_corners.** A public function,
  `cucim.skimage.measure.oriented_bbox_corners(props)`, returns the `2**ndim` corners of the
  oriented boxes for all labels from the result of `regionprops_dict` or `regionprops_table` (NumPy
  or CuPy; absent labels are NaN). It raises a `ValueError` that lists the properties that were not
  requested.
- **min_area_bbox_size, min_area_bbox_center, min_area_bbox_angle (2D).** The rectangle of the
  smallest area that encloses the same polygon as the Feret diameters (it has a side along a hull
  edge, Freeman and Shapira 1975).
  - The size is (length, width) with length ≥ width, the center is in the coordinates of `centroid`,
    and the angle is that of the length side, in the convention of `feret_angle_min`.
  - The corners are `min_area_bbox_corners(props)`, in the same way.
  - Unlike the oriented box it does not depend on the mass distribution: a square rotated by 45
    degrees gets the box with its own sides. Neither ITK nor DIPlib has this (DIPlib's `Feret` gives
    `Min` and `PerpMin`, which are usually, but not necessarily, the sides of the minimum bounding
    box).

The Feret values and `perimeter_convex` are measured on the same polygon as the existing
`feret_diameter_max`: the hull of the convex image's pixel-edge midpoints, which is scikit-image's
contour of the convex image. DIPlib uses the hull of the region's own pixel-edge midpoints, which is
slightly smaller. On the library comparison's test ellipse, for example, the maximum diameter is
24.19 there against 24.60 here. Using the convex image's hull keeps the maximum and minimum
diameters, their angles and their ratio consistent with `feret_diameter_max`.

## Comparison with ITK and DIPlib

### Definitions

| Property | cuCIM (this PR) | ITK (`ShapeLabelMapFilter`, SimpleITK `LabelShapeStatisticsImageFilter`) | DIPlib (`MeasurementTool`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `surface_area` (3D) | Crofton, 13 directions; weights recomputed for anisotropic spacing | `Perimeter`: the same estimate, with the isotropic weights for every spacing | `SurfaceArea`: another estimator, weights for Mullikin's surface-voxel configurations |
| `feret_diameter_min`, `_min_perpendicular`, angles (2D) | rotating calipers on the convex image's hull | — (`FeretDiameter` is the maximum only, by brute force over pairs of boundary pixels) | `Feret`: rotating calipers on the region's hull |
| `perimeter_convex` (2D) | length of the same hull | — | `ConvexPerimeter` |
| `oriented_bbox_size`, `_center` | principal-axes box enclosing the pixels; size and center | `OrientedBoundingBox`: the same box; size, a corner (origin) and the directions | — (`DimensionsCube` is a box with the same moments, not an enclosing box) |
| minimum-area rectangle | — | — | — (`Min` × `PerpMin` is the box at the minimum-width direction) |

Neither ITK or DIPlib computes a minimum-area enclosing rectangle. For 21 of 200 random convex polygons,
the box at the minimum-width direction (DIPlib's `Min` × `PerpMin`, and MorphoLibJ's
`OrientedBoundingBox2D`) was larger than the minimum-area rectangle, by up to 10%.

### Agreement

`regionprops-perf/shape_extras_check.py export <dir>` writes label images and cuCIM's values.
`compare <dir>` computes the same quantities with SimpleITK 2.5.6 and DIPlib 3.6.1, in a separate
environment:

- **surface_area.** The largest relative difference from SimpleITK's `Perimeter` is 7e-14–9e-14, for
  touching random labels and for ellipsoids, with isotropic spacing. This holds on the benchmark
  tilings below as well (9e-14, up to 3971 labels).
  - With spacing (0.5, 1.5, 0.8) the values differ by up to 18% (random labels) and 26%
    (ellipsoids), by design, since commit 5. Before commit 5 they agreed to 1e-13 there too.
  - Against the exact areas of those ellipsoids (Legendre's formula), ITK's weights read 20–29% too
    small, the recomputed ones 7–11% too small.
- **Oriented bounding box.** The largest relative size difference is 4e-13. The largest center
  difference, against the mean of ITK's vertices, is 8e-12. This covers 2D (42 blob regions and 5
  shapes) and 3D (7 regions), with isotropic and anisotropic spacing. Labels with equal principal
  moments (to 1e-6) have arbitrary axes and are skipped: 10 of 108 comparisons.
- **Feret values.** DIPlib is given each region's convex image as a one-label image, so that its
  hull is the same polygon as cuCIM's.
  - On 42 blob regions and 5 hand-made shapes, cuCIM's five values equal a brute-force computation
    on that polygon (ties accepted).
  - DIPlib's `Max`, `MaxAng` (up to ties) and `ConvexPerimeter` (4e-16) agree.
  - DIPlib's `Min`, `MinAng` and `PerpMin` are wrong for 2 of the 42 blobs: `Min` is 22.90 instead
    of 21.99, and 31.00 instead of 27.04. DIPlib's calipers loop does not measure the width at the
    edges that its first pointer walks along (`ConvexHull::Feret` in `measure_polygon.cpp`). This is
    documented in section 5 of the library comparison and has not been reported upstream yet.

## Performance

**Setup.**
- **Hardware.** An NVIDIA RTX A6000 (CuPy 14.2, CUDA 13) and an Intel Core i9-10980XE (18 cores, 36
  threads).
- **Libraries.** scikit-image 0.26 runs on one thread. SimpleITK 2.5.6 and DIPlib 3.6.1 use their
  default of 20 threads.
- **Inputs.** The tilings of the regionprops explainer: 3840 × 2160 with 64, 1024 or 16 256 labels,
  and 192³ with 8, 498 or 3971 labels. Each is a tiling of disks, ellipses, squares and plus shapes
  (2D), or balls, ellipsoids, cuboids and 3D plus shapes (3D), with isotropic spacing unless noted.
- **Timing.** cuCIM's times are the median CUDA-event times of
  `regionprops_table(..., copy_output_to_host=True)`, over 20 runs after 0.3 s of warm-up. CPU times
  are wall-clock means of up to 3 runs.
- **Script.** `regionprops-perf/shape_enhancements_bench.py`: `gpu <dir>` for cuCIM and
  scikit-image, then `cpu <dir>` for SimpleITK and DIPlib in the comparison environment. The results
  are in `regionprops-perf/shape_enhancements_*.csv`. The cuCIM times below come from a
  re-measurement on an idle CPU (`..._gpu_rerun.csv`). Its two runs agree to about 2%, except
  `feret_diameter_max` with 64 labels (1.23–1.66 ms). The `surface_area` times were measured again
  after commit 7 (`..._gpu_surface_cache.csv`, two runs within 2%).

### Against scikit-image

scikit-image has none of these properties, so each comparison uses the closest scikit-image
computation:

- **Feret values.** scikit-image's `feret_diameter_max`, its only Feret value. It builds the same
  hull, so its time is a lower bound for a scikit-image-based computation of all five values.
- **Oriented box.** scikit-image's `regionprops`, with a NumPy projection of `coords_scaled` onto
  the eigenvectors of `inertia_tensor`. This gives the same box. It equals cuCIM's to 1e-12, except
  for labels with equal principal moments, whose box is arbitrary. For example, 11 of the 498 3D
  labels differ, all with two principal moments equal to within 2e-16 (relative).
- **Surface area.** `marching_cubes` and `mesh_surface_area` on each region's padded image,
  scikit-image's usual way to measure a surface. It is another estimator: its areas are 5.7–7.9%
  larger than `surface_area` (median per image).

2D, 3840 × 2160:

| Labels | cuCIM: 5 Feret values + `perimeter_convex` | cuCIM: `feret_diameter_max` alone | scikit-image `feret_diameter_max` | Speedup (6 values) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 | 1.64 ms | 1.23 ms | 484 ms | 295× |
| 1024 | 1.04 ms | 0.75 ms | 1038 ms | 998× |
| 16 256 | 1.14 ms | 0.77 ms | 6835 ms | 6001× |

| Labels | cuCIM oriented box | scikit-image `regionprops` + NumPy | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 | 0.79 ms | 181 ms | 230× |
| 1024 | 0.83 ms | 551 ms | 662× |
| 16 256 | 1.40 ms | 4915 ms | 3503× |

3D, 192³:

| Labels | cuCIM oriented box | scikit-image `regionprops` + NumPy | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 | 0.76 ms | 65 ms | 86× |
| 498 | 0.85 ms | 319 ms | 377× |
| 3971 | 0.99 ms | 1642 ms | 1652× |

| Labels | cuCIM `surface_area` | cuCIM, spacing (2, 1, 1) | scikit-image marching cubes per region | Speedup (isotropic) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 | 0.23 ms | 0.30 ms | 70 ms | 311× |
| 498 | 0.28 ms | 0.50 ms | 369 ms | 1332× |
| 3971 | 0.29 ms | 0.54 ms | 1075 ms | 3693× |

The five Feret values and the convex perimeter cost 0.3–0.4 ms more than `feret_diameter_max` alone.
The calipers add one thread per label over the hull that `feret_diameter_max` already builds. The
64-label image, which has the largest labels, is the slowest for both. With anisotropic spacing,
`surface_area` counts the neighbors in 13 groups instead of 3, which takes 0.07–0.25 ms more.

### Against SimpleITK and DIPlib

These compute the same or similar values on the CPU, multithreaded:

| Image | Labels | cuCIM | SimpleITK (20 threads) | DIPlib (20 threads) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Feret + convex perimeter** | | | | `Feret` + `ConvexPerimeter` |
| 3840 × 2160 | 64 | 1.64 ms | — | 28.9 ms (18×) |
| 3840 × 2160 | 1024 | 1.04 ms | — | 36.3 ms (35×) |
| 3840 × 2160 | 16 256 | 1.14 ms | — | 91.5 ms (80×) |
| **Oriented box** | | | oriented bounding box | |
| 3840 × 2160 | 64 | 0.79 ms | 7.7 ms (10×) | — |
| 3840 × 2160 | 1024 | 0.83 ms | 13.1 ms (16×) | — |
| 3840 × 2160 | 16 256 | 1.40 ms | 62.6 ms (45×) | — |
| 192³ | 8 | 0.76 ms | 6.4 ms (8×) | — |
| 192³ | 498 | 0.85 ms | 13.7 ms (16×) | — |
| 192³ | 3971 | 0.99 ms | 22.9 ms (23×) | — |
| **Surface area** | | | `Perimeter` | `SurfaceArea` |
| 192³ | 8 | 0.23 ms | 20.4 ms (91×) | 153 ms (680×) |
| 192³ | 498 | 0.28 ms | 23.5 ms (85×) | 148 ms (533×) |
| 192³ | 3971 | 0.29 ms | 44.7 ms (154×) | 152 ms (521×) |

The speedups in parentheses are relative to cuCIM's time in the same row. Notes on the comparison:

- SimpleITK cannot compute a single property. Its times include the conversion to a label map and
  the basic shape statistics, which alone take 5.3–62 ms on these images (`ComputePerimeter` and
  `ComputeOrientedBoundingBox` off). So the oriented box itself adds little there, and `Perimeter`
  adds 11–16 ms.
- With spacing (2, 1, 1), SimpleITK's `Perimeter` takes 19–47 ms, against cuCIM's 0.30–0.54 ms
  (38–89×). Its values differ from cuCIM's there, because of the recomputed weights.
- DIPlib's `Feret` is computed on the region's own hull, and its `SurfaceArea` is another estimator.
  The times compare the work, not identical values.

## Commits

### 1. Add a batch surface_area for 3D regions

A new kind of the label-aware boundary kernels (`_get_surface_area_op`): one label-run pass, 10
pixels per thread, in which a boundary voxel tests its 26 neighbors. The neighbors without the
voxel's label are counted in integers, per group of directions with the same weight: 3 groups with
isotropic spacing, 13 otherwise. A boundary voxel then needs 3 or 13 double-precision multiply-adds
instead of 26 conditional ones, which made the pass 1.5–1.9× faster on the 3D benchmark images. A 2D
image raises `ValueError`, through a new set `ndim_3_only`.

GPU time of `regionprops_dict` for one property, measured when the commit was written (median of 20
runs after a 0.3 s warm-up; tilings of balls, ellipsoids, boxes and plus shapes):

| Image | Labels | `euler_number` | `surface_area` | `surface_area`, spacing (0.5, 1.5, 0.8) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 192³ | 8 | 0.246 ms | 0.323 ms | 0.451 ms |
| 192³ | 498 | 0.309 ms | 0.386 ms | 0.667 ms |
| 192³ | 3971 | 0.325 ms | 0.401 ms | 0.697 ms |

Tests:
- against a NumPy reference (2 label types, 2 spacings, touching random labels and blobs, an absent
  label);
- a digitized ball of radius 20 against 4πr² (within 1%);
- the weights against `SphericalVoronoi`;
- the 2D error.

### 2. Add the minimum Feret diameter and Feret angles in 2D

A new kernel, `_get_feret_calipers_2d_kernel`, runs rotating calipers (Preparata and Shamos, 1985)
with one thread per label. It works on the vertices of the hull chains that the 2D Feret kernel
already builds:

- for each edge, a pointer advances to the vertex farthest from the edge's line (at most twice
  around the polygon in total); that distance is the polygon's width normal to the edge, and the
  smallest width is the minimum Feret diameter;
- the vertices the pointer passes, with the edge's ends (and the other end of a parallel edge), are
  the antipodal pairs, among which the largest distance is the maximum Feret diameter and gives its
  angle;
- the extent of the vertices along the edge of the minimum width is the perpendicular width.

Coordinates are scaled by the spacing. Absent labels get 0 widths and NaN angles.

Test: `test_feret_calipers_2d`, against a brute-force computation on scikit-image's convex images
(all maximal and minimal ties accepted), for blobs, thin lines and multi-component labels, with and
without anisotropic spacing.

### 3. Add the perimeter of the convex hull in 2D

The calipers kernel also adds up the edge lengths of the polygon, so `perimeter_convex` costs
nothing more when the Feret properties are computed. Tested against the perimeter of scipy's
`ConvexHull` of the convex image's pixel-edge midpoints.

### 4. Add the oriented bounding box

A projection is linear, so the extremes of the pixel centers along an axis are at the first or last
pixel of some row. The convex-hull properties' row-extent pass already finds those pixels.
- One thread per row of each bounding box projects the row's two end pixel centers onto the label's
  axes, and keeps the extremes per label with atomics.
- One thread per label then widens the box by the extent of one pixel along each axis,
  `Σ_d |V[d, a]| · spacing[d]`, and computes the center.
- The row extents are shared with the convex-hull properties when both are requested.

The atomics are `cucim_atomic_min` and `cucim_atomic_max` from the shared kernel preamble, added by
commit 22 of the bug-fix PR. CuPy 14.2's `atomicMin` and `atomicMax` overloads for `double`
(`cupy/_core/include/cupy/atomics.cuh`) compare with `fminf` and `fmaxf`, the single-precision
functions. So they round the stored values to float precision; with them, the box was off by about
1e-6.

Tests:
- against a NumPy projection of all pixel centers (2D and 3D, two spacings, two kinds of labels);
- the documented corner formula, which must enclose every pixel corner and touch the extremes along
  each axis;
- absent labels (NaN);
- a rotated 51 × 17 rectangle.

### 5. Compute the surface_area weights for the voxel spacing

Commit 1 weighted the 13 directions as ITK does, with the Voronoi cells of a cubic grid's
directions, also for anisotropic spacing. Lang, Ohser and Hilfer, who derive these weights, note
that they are accurate only for equal lattice distances or isotropic structures. The weights are now
the areas of the Voronoi cells of the spacing-scaled directions, computed with
`scipy.spatial.SphericalVoronoi`. That takes 0.7 ms on the host per spacing, then the result is
cached. Isotropic spacing keeps ITK's constants. The kernel is unchanged.

A flat face with normal `n` is measured times `2 · Σ_k c_k |u_k · n|`, where the `u_k` are the unit
directions and the `c_k` their weights. The exact range of this factor over all orientations:

| Spacing | ITK's weights | Spacing-aware weights |
|---|---|---|
| (1, 1, 1) | 0.927–1.023 | 0.927–1.023 |
| (2, 1, 1) | 0.755–1.250 | 0.874–1.094 |
| (1, 2, 2) | 0.635–1.140 | 0.842–1.071 |
| (5, 1, 1) | 0.559–1.375 | 0.768–1.100 |

Measured as `surface_area` / true area, before → after:
- **Plates** of 8 × 240 × 240 (physical units):
  - spacing (2, 1, 1), normal to axis 0: 1.140 → 0.894;
  - spacing (2, 1, 1), normal to axis 2: 0.763 → 0.891;
  - spacing (1, 2, 2), normal to axis 0: 0.655 → 0.842;
  - spacing (1, 2, 2), normal to axis 2: 1.013 → 0.916.
- **Ellipsoids** of `shape_extras_check.py`, spacing (0.5, 1.5, 0.8), against Legendre's exact area:
  0.71–0.81 → 0.89–0.93.
- **Balls** are unbiased with either weights (radius 60: within 0.2% for spacing (2, 1, 1) and (5,
  1, 1)). With (5, 1, 1) and radius 20, only 4 voxels along axis 0: 1.007 → 1.016.

The docstrings of `regionprops_dict` and `regionprops_surface_area` now state these accuracy limits.

Tests:
- the NumPy reference uses the Voronoi weights of each spacing;
- the weights for 4 spacings, against the share of a Fibonacci lattice of 2²⁰ points on the sphere
  nearest to each direction (to 1e-4);
- a box test: axis-aligned plates and an unequal box, with 3 spacings, must equal the closed-form
  intercept count to 1e-12, and lie within 2.5% below the area predicted from their faces' factors.

### 6. Document that the oriented box is not the smallest box

Documentation only. The principal-axes box is in general larger than the smallest enclosing box:
1.059 times the smallest rectangle for a right triangle with legs of 200 and 100 pixels. With equal
principal moments it is arbitrary. A square rotated by 45 degrees keeps an axis-aligned box of twice
its area, and a rotated cube of side 60 got 4.3 times its volume.

### 7. Cache the surface_area coefficients for each spacing

`surface_area` computed its 3 or 13 direction coefficients on the host, and copied them to the
device, on every call. That took 0.08–0.14 ms, longer than measuring a 64³ image. The device array
is now memoized per device and spacing, as the perimeter and Crofton coefficients already were. The
spacing is first normalized to a tuple of floats, so any sequence, or None, can be passed. The
values are unchanged.

A/B against commit 6: the median GPU time of `regionprops_dict` with `surface_area`, best of 3
alternating runs (RTX A6000), on the tilings of `bench_regionprops.py`:

| Image | Labels | Spacing | Before | After | Speedup |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 64³ | 8 | isotropic | 0.116 ms | 0.037 ms | 3.15× |
| 64³ | 8 | (2, 1, 1) | 0.186 ms | 0.047 ms | 3.96× |
| 192³ | 8 | isotropic | 0.202 ms | 0.121 ms | 1.67× |
| 192³ | 8 | (2, 1, 1) | 0.329 ms | 0.194 ms | 1.70× |
| 192³ | 498 | isotropic | 0.256 ms | 0.174 ms | 1.47× |
| 192³ | 498 | (2, 1, 1) | 0.530 ms | 0.393 ms | 1.35× |
| 192³ | 3971 | isotropic | 0.266 ms | 0.184 ms | 1.44× |
| 192³ | 3971 | (2, 1, 1) | 0.563 ms | 0.422 ms | 1.33× |

The `surface_area` times in the performance tables above were measured after this commit.

Test: `test_surface_area_spacing_types` checks that tuple, list and NumPy spacings give the same
values, and that None gives those of unit spacing. The comparison allows a relative 1e-14, since the
order of the double-precision atomic additions varies between runs.

### 8. Add oriented_bbox_corners

The corners follow from the size, the center and the eigenvectors,
`center + Σ_a ±size[a]/2 · V[:, a]`, which users had to write themselves. The function takes the
result of `regionprops_dict` or `regionprops_table` (the columns of a table are stacked back into
arrays; `separator` is a keyword), and returns the corners of all labels in the order of
`itertools.product([-1, 1], repeat=ndim)`. A `ValueError` lists the missing properties and says to
request them in `properties`.

Tests:
- `test_oriented_bbox_corners` (4): the corners against an explicit loop over the sign choices, the
  box frame's extremes, NaN for absent labels, and the order 0, 1, 3, 2 around the rectangle in 2D;
- `test_oriented_bbox_corners_table` (4): the columns of `regionprops_table` with two separators, on
  the host and on the device, give the same corners;
- `test_oriented_bbox_corners_missing_properties`: the `ValueError`.

### 9. Add the minimum-area enclosing rectangle of 2D regions

The calipers kernel (commit 2) visits every hull edge with its farthest vertex. Two more pointers,
which only move forward, find the vertices with the largest and smallest position along the edge.
The rectangle with a side on that edge is then width × extent, and the smallest of these is kept,
with its center, size and angle. Only hull edges need to be tried (Freeman and Shapira).

The kernel always computes the box when it runs for the other Feret properties. For the minimum
Feret diameter alone this costs 0.59 → 0.65 ms for 32 × 32 tiles of a 2160 × 3840 image, and 2.85 →
3.72 ms for one disc of radius 900 (a hull of many vertices, on one thread).

Tests:
- `test_min_area_bbox_2d` (6): size, center and angle against a brute-force search over the edges of
  the hull of the convex image's pixel-edge midpoints (any of the tied optimal edges), with two
  spacings and three kinds of labels; NaN for absent labels;
- `test_min_area_bbox_rotated_square`: the sides of a square rotated by 45 degrees;
- `test_min_area_bbox_corners` (6): `min_area_bbox_corners(props)` gives a rectangle of the size,
  around the center, with the first axis along the angle, that encloses the Feret polygon, with NaN
  for absent labels;
- `test_min_area_bbox_corners_table_and_missing`: the columns of a table, and the `ValueError` that
  lists the missing properties.

`min_area_bbox_corners(props)` returns the corners of the rectangles like
`oriented_bbox_corners(props)` does for the oriented boxes (the rotation of the angle is the axes),
with the same `ValueError` for properties that were not requested.

## Bugs found while doing this

- **CuPy's double-precision atomicMin and atomicMax** (see commit 4). The batch `intensity_min` and
  `intensity_max` of float64 intensity images used them, so they were rounded to float32 precision.
  That is fixed in the bug-fix PR, which adds the `cucim_atomic_min` and  `cucim_atomic_max` helpers
  this PR uses. CuPy's development version still has the single-precision comparisons, and CuPy
  should be told.
- **DIPlib's minimum Feret width** (see "Agreement" above).

## Provenance

The definitions follow ITK's `ShapeLabelMapFilter` (surface area, oriented bounding box) and
DIPlib's `Feret` and `ConvexPerimeter` features. Their sources (Apache-2.0) were read to describe
them in the library comparison. No code was copied:
- the Crofton weights were computed independently, for anisotropic spacing as Lang, Ohser and Hilfer
  propose;
- the rotating calipers follow the standard description (Preparata and Shamos, *Computational
  Geometry: An Introduction*, Springer 1985, cited from DIPlib's source code), with the width
  checked at every edge.

title: Faster color conversions for float32 and 8/16-bit images
body:
## Summary

The conversions of `cucim.skimage.color` were far from memory bound, for two reasons:

1. **Double precision arithmetic on float32 data.** The element-wise kernels contain floating point
   literals such as `0.04045`, `12.92`, `7.787` and the entries of the conversion matrices. In C++
   these are `double` literals, so for a `float32` array every expression was evaluated in double
   precision and rounded when it was stored. That runs at the FP64 rate of the GPU, which is 1/64 of
   the FP32 rate on the RTX A6000 used here (check the rate of other GPUs). It affects every input
   that gives a `float32` result: 8 and 16-bit integers, `float16` and `float32`.
2. **Extra passes over the image.** Several conversions copied the input and then changed the copy
   in place, converted 8 and 16-bit input in a separate pass before the conversion kernel, ran
   `rgb2lab` and `lab2rgb` as two kernels with an intermediate array, and clipped the result of
   `rgb2hed` in another pass. A float32 pass over a 2048 × 2048 × 3 image takes about 0.15 ms, so
   each of these cost as much as a conversion.

After this PR `rgb2lab` of a 2048 × 2048 float32 image takes 0.18 ms instead of 1.9 ms (0.13 ms
instead of 1.8 ms for a `uint8` image), `rgb2hed` 0.17 ms instead of 2.0 ms, and most of the
conversions are at the time of one read and one write of the image. The results of the commits that
remove passes are the same as before, up to two rounding-level exceptions (see "Accuracy"), and
`float64` input is unaffected.

## Commits

1. **color: compute float32 conversions in single precision.** `color/_kernel_utils.py`
   (`typed_float_literals`, which casts the literals of a kernel's source, its operation and its
   preamble, to the data type `X`, and `elementwise_kernel`), used by the 13 kernels of
   `colorconv.py`. The float32 results change in the last bits (see "Accuracy").
2. **Seed the random images of `test_structural_similarity_dtype`.** Unrelated to the colors, and
   can be taken separately. The test drew random images from the global NumPy state (which depends
   on which tests ran before it) and asserted `SSIM < 0.1` for two independent random images, which
   is false for about 0.3% of the draws; it failed once while I was running the tests for this PR
   and passed when run again. It now uses a seeded generator (the value is -0.03, far from the
   threshold). The integer dtypes also built `Y` from `X`, so that case compared an image with a
   transformed copy of itself and passed trivially; `Y` is now built from `Y`.
3. **color: do not copy the input before converting it.** `rgb2xyz`, `xyz2lab`, `ycbcr2rgb`,
   `lab2lch` and `lch2lab` copied the input and changed the copy in place. The convert kernels now
   apply their pre and post steps to local variables, and `lab2lch` and `lch2lab` read the input and
   write the output. Inputs are never modified (tested).
4. **color: convert 8 and 16-bit and float16 input inside the kernels.** The kernels of the convert
   family (`rgb2xyz`, and so `rgb2lab` and `rgb2luv`, the YUV family, `rgb2rgbcie`), `rgb2hsv`,
   `rgb2gray` and `separate_stains` (`rgb2hed`) read `uint8`, `uint16` and `float16` arrays directly
   and apply the factor of `img_as_float` (`float32(1 / 255)` or `float32(1 / 65535)`) while they
   load the values, instead of a separate pass that writes a float32 copy. Other dtypes are
   converted as before.
5. **color: convert rgb2lab and lab2rgb in one kernel.** `rgb2lab` is the `rgb2xyz` kernel with the
   XYZ to Lab step as its post-processing code, and `lab2rgb` the `xyz2rgb` kernel with the Lab to
   XYZ step as its pre-processing code. The negative-Z warning of `lab2xyz` and `lab2rgb` counted
   the invalid pixels with a full-size int32 array and a `count_nonzero` pass; the kernels now add
   to one int32 counter, with one atomic add per warp that has an invalid pixel. The number in the
   warning is the same. Reading the count still synchronizes with the device, as before.
6. **color: clip the stain values inside the separate_stains kernel.** The `cp.maximum` pass over
   the result of `rgb2hed` is done in the kernel.
7. **color: convert rgb2luv and luv2rgb in one kernel.** The same mechanism as commit 5: the XYZ to
   Luv step (with its helper functions in the kernel's preamble) is the post-processing code of the
   `rgb2xyz` kernel, and the Luv to XYZ step the pre-processing code of the `xyz2rgb` kernel.
   `xyz2luv` and `luv2xyz` use the same code.

**Commit 1 changes the float32 results in the last bits.** They are computed in single instead of
double precision. Measured against the float64 result of the same function on the same values (table
above), the largest absolute error is below 1e-6 (4.5e-7 or less) for most of the functions with
values up to 1 and is a few 1e-6 to 2.5e-5 for `lab2rgb` (6.6e-6; 5.5e-6 before), `xyz2rgb` (2.7e-6;
2.0e-6 before) and `luv2rgb` (2.4e-5; 1.3e-5 before). It is 2.7e-5 for `rgb2ycbcr` (values up to
240; 1.1e-5 before) and 6.4e-5 to 7.6e-5 for Lab (values up to 108; 6.5e-5 to 6.6e-5 before) and
1.3e-4 for Luv (values up to 175; 6.0e-5 before), a relative error below 1e-6. `lab2lch` and
`lch2lab` (values around 100) are unchanged, at 1.5e-5 and 3.5e-5. So the error stays at the level
of the float32 spacing, and some functions go up by a factor of two or less. Code that thresholds or
compares converted values can change on near-ties, for a few pixels. The `float64` path is not
changed (its literals were already `double`).

**Commits 3 to 7 do not change any result, with two exceptions that are at the level of rounding.**
I compared 182 outputs (every conversion function, for `uint8`, `uint16`, `int8`, `int16`, `int32`,
`float16`, `float32` and `float64` inputs, contiguous and not, and the 5-channel `lab2lch` and
`lch2lab`) before and after each commit: they are bit for bit equal, with two exceptions that come
from the compiler contracting the multiply-adds differently once the values are in registers instead
of in an array: in commit 3 about 10% of the values of `yuv2rgb` (float64) and `ycbcr2rgb` differ by
one ulp, and in commit 7 `luv2rgb` differs from the two-step result for about 17% of the values of a
random image, by at most 1.5e-6. For `luv2rgb` the Luv to XYZ formula is ill-conditioned near black;
the error against the float64 result is the same as before (mean 2.1e-7, at most 1.9e-5 against
1.85e-5).

  values untouched, a preamble); float32 results against float64 for every `rgb2*` function; float32

  it (one or two conversions of each kind of kernel, 15 in all, for `uint8`, `float32` and `float64`

  fused `rgb2lab` and `lab2rgb` equal the two-step conversions, bit for bit, for other illuminants
  and observers; the count in the negative-Z warning; the clipping of `separate_stains`.
- All 691 tests of `cucim/skimage/color` pass (the existing ones compare with scikit-image).
- Functions that use the conversions internally (`label2rgb`, `equalize_adapthist`, `blur_effect`,

  modules that call the conversions on their data, were run, not only the `color` tests:

  `measure/test_blur_effect`, `filters`, `morphology`, `transform` and `core` (10,599 passed, 44
  skipped).

title: Add SLIC superpixels (SLIC, SLIC0 and maskSLIC)
body:
## Summary

This PR adds `cucim.skimage.segmentation.slic`, a GPU implementation of SLIC superpixel segmentation
with the API of `skimage.segmentation.slic`. It resolves #855. It supports 2D and 3D images,
grayscale and multichannel input with any `channel_axis`, `start_label`, SLIC0 (`slic_zero=True`)
and maskSLIC (`mask=...`), and it is 190 to 640 times faster than scikit-image for SLIC and SLIC0
on the sizes benchmarked below (23 to 245 times for maskSLIC, which has a more expensive
initialization).

The kernels started from the 3D CUDA SLIC implementation in `cuda-slic` (Apache-2.0; that project
has only a 3D kernel, and the 2D kernel was obtained by reducing the dimensionality of the 3D one),
and have been substantially refactored. The attribution is in `LICENSE-3rdparty.md` and in the
headers of the kernel files.

The PR also adds the utility `cucim.skimage.util.regular_grid`, which `slic` uses

## What is added

- **`cucim.skimage.segmentation.slic`**, with the arguments of scikit-image's `slic` and these
  cuCIM-specific keyword-only options (documented under `Other Parameters`):
  `maximization_algorithm` (`"atomic"`, the default, or the original scan-based `"scan"`),
  `connectivity_algorithm` (`"gpu"`, the default, or `"host"`, which uses scikit-image's Cython
  cleanup), `relabel_connectivity` (dense sequential labels after the GPU cleanup, on by default),
  `force_kmeans2` (use SciPy's `kmeans2` for the initial maskSLIC centroids even if cuVS is
  installed) and `rng_on_host` (sample the maskSLIC seed points on the host with scikit-image's
  `RandomState(123)`; off by default).
- **`cucim.skimage.util.regular_grid`**.
- **Tests** adapted from scikit-image's, plus tests of the cuCIM-specific behavior (see "Testing").
- **Benchmarks**: the SLIC cases of `benchmarks/skimage/cucim_segmentation_bench.py`.

## Implementation notes

The core iteration runs on the GPU as an assignment kernel (expectation) and a center update
(maximization). The update uses atomic accumulation of the center sums by default, as 64-bit
fixed-point integers, so its labels are identical from run to run; the scan path sums in floating
point, so the two can differ slightly in the centers they compute.

The assignment kernels select the candidate centers once per thread block (in grid order, so ties
are broken as in scikit-image) instead of once per pixel, and the atomic updates combine equal-label
runs across a warp before issuing atomics. A pixel is assigned to the closest center whose window
(+- 2 grid steps around the current center) contains it, as in scikit-image, and pixels in no window
keep their previous label. The search for such centers covers `2 + 4` grid cells on each side, which
reproduces scikit-image's labels before connectivity cleanup to within a few pixels down to
compactness 0.3 (astronaut image, 400 segments).

- **SLIC0** adapts the color distance scale per cluster (a per-cluster maximum, updated with warp
  combining).
- **maskSLIC** computes superpixels only within a mask and assigns pixels outside it to
  `start_label - 1`. The initial centroids use cuVS k-means when cuVS is available, with SciPy's
  `kmeans2` as the fallback (a `RuntimeWarning` is emitted once per process when the fallback is
  used because cuVS is missing or fails; `force_kmeans2=True` is silent). The random mask
  coordinates that seed the centroids are sampled on the GPU by default; `rng_on_host=True` samples
  them on the host as scikit-image does, which takes about 100 ms for a mask of 2.5 million pixels.
- **Connectivity cleanup** (`enforce_connectivity=True`, the default) runs on the GPU: connected
  components, then repeated merging of components that are too small, until none is left. It avoids
  copying the label image to the host. Its small-component merge policy is not identical to
  scikit-image's (see "Compatibility"). Dense sequential relabeling follows by default;
  `relabel_connectivity=False` skips it (call `relabel_sequential` later if dense labels are
  needed).
- **Color conversion.** For RGB `uint8` and `float32` images that are converted to Lab (the
  default), the rescaling to [0, 1], the RGB to Lab conversion and the weighting by
  `1 / compactness` are done in one single-precision kernel (private to `slic`) instead of about
  eight separate passes. The compiled kernels are cached between calls, so small images are not
  limited by the per-call overhead.

## Commits

The 42 commits, in order, grouped by what they do:

1. **Port and scaffolding** (`4e07178e` to `414467c4`): `regular_grid`, the port of the `cuda-slic`
   kernels with clang-format and refactoring, the scikit-image tests enabled and fixed, `float32`
   and `float64` input; SLIC0 and maskSLIC raise `NotImplementedError` until they are added.
2. **Kernel performance** (`e076f704` to `3ad2fea2`): 32-bit distance arithmetic, `__restrict__` and
   unrolling, a launch configuration fix for the 2D kernel, no unneeded synchronizations, and the
   batched pixel atomic center update (made the default, `3ad2fea2`).
3. **SLIC0, maskSLIC and GPU connectivity** (`36fe8dd6` to `e1b98cfc`): SLIC0, maskSLIC (and the
   removal of the SciPy `kmeans2` bottleneck of its initialization), and the GPU connectivity
   cleanup.
4. **Licensing and references** (`f1ac4f0a`, `8b64cc6a`, `983f4fa3`): license notes and copyright
   headers, and the SLIC, SLIC0 and maskSLIC references in the docstring.
5. **Agreement with scikit-image** (`ce2e2d77`, `5576c1c4`, `f9c5846c`, `a115f2a3`, `d8a3e2b3`,
   `2180f433`, `778038da`): any `channel_axis`, scikit-image's search window for maskSLIC, constant
   images and 3-element 2D arguments, the assignment and update windows, only adding pixel colors
   inside the center window, a `regular_grid` fix, and repeating the GPU merge until no component is
   too small.
6. **Deterministic and faster updates** (`482459ba`, `68ed0817`, `65ee033b`, `43d9d321`, `5f03e067`,
   `d2d03ac9`): warp combining of equal-label runs in the atomic update and in SLIC0, fixed-point
   sums for run-to-run identical labels, one candidate-center selection per block (also for the mask
   kernel), and 4 extra grid cells searched by default.
7. **maskSLIC initialization and options** (`6c7ddcd6`, `3887ea0a`, `b3824fb4`, `d4b25925`): the
   cuVS and `kmeans2` difference documented, `rng_on_host`, the one-time fallback warning and cuVS
   in the test dependencies, and the k-means subsample size difference documented.
8. **Benchmarks and call overhead** (`41f9eb43`, `ced6f5f0`, `d275afa5`): the benchmark script
   updates, the masked benchmark with the GPU connectivity, and the fused color conversion with
   cached kernels.

## Benchmarks

NVIDIA RTX A6000, Intel Core i9-10980XE, scikit-image on the CPU. `float32` images,
`max_num_iter=10`, from `benchmarks/skimage/cucim_segmentation_bench.py -f slic` (summarized by
`summarize_slic_bench.py`). "GPU host ms" and "GPU device ms" are the host and device times of the
cuCIM call; the speedup is CPU time over GPU device time.

- The **unmasked** tables use `enforce_connectivity=False` (compactness 25 for SLIC, 10 for SLIC0),
  on both sides, so they time the iterations and not the connectivity cleanup; the cost of the
  cleanup is in "Connectivity cleanup" below.
- The **masked** tables use `enforce_connectivity=True` with `connectivity_algorithm="gpu"`, and the
  cuVS centroid initialization.
- The CPU times are from one full run (3 s per case). The GPU times are the mean of two GPU-only
  runs made one after the other with the same script, because the GPU times of the full run varied
  by up to 40% between neighboring cases; the two runs agree to within a few percent. The
  `rng_on_host=True` tables use `cupyx.profiler.benchmark` on the same data and arguments (the
  script is not part of the benchmark file) and the CPU times of the default tables.

Speedups over scikit-image (device time): SLIC 2D 190 to 414 times, SLIC0 2D 179 to 309 times, SLIC
3D 234 to 639 times, SLIC0 3D 201 to 454 times, maskSLIC 41 to 245 times (24 to 89 times with

default gives different seed points than scikit-image, so its labels differ from scikit-image's.


## Compatibility

The public API is intended to be broadly compatible with `skimage.segmentation.slic`, while adding
cuCIM-specific keyword-only controls for performance and implementation selection. Known behavior
differences are in implementation details where exact scikit-image behavior is not guaranteed:

- **GPU connectivity cleanup** (`connectivity_algorithm="gpu"`, the default) is qualitatively
  similar but not label-identical, because it uses a GPU-friendly small-component merge policy;
  `connectivity_algorithm="host"` uses scikit-image's cleanup. Before the cleanup the labels agree
  with scikit-image's to within a few pixels down to compactness 0.3, and with
  `connectivity_algorithm="host"` the final labels are identical to scikit-image's at compactness 10
  and above and in 3D, in the cases tested.
- **maskSLIC centroids**: cuVS k-means converges to slightly different centroids than
  `scipy.cluster.vq.kmeans2` (about 0.7% of the pixels differ in the case tested), and the default
  `rng_on_host=False` samples different seed points than scikit-image. `rng_on_host=True` together
  with `force_kmeans2=True` gives labels that match scikit-image before the connectivity cleanup.
- **Arithmetic**: single-precision sums, the single-precision Lab conversion (its values differ from
  a double precision conversion by up to about 1e-5) and the fixed-point center update can differ
  from scikit-image's float64 arithmetic in rare ties.

## Testing

- `segmentation/tests/test_slic.py`: the scikit-image tests, adapted, and tests of the
  cuCIM-specific behavior (the options above, the atomic and scan paths, the GPU and host
  connectivity, SLIC0, maskSLIC with and without cuVS, `channel_axis`, constant images, 2D and 3D,
  single and double precision, run-to-run determinism, and the fused color conversion against the
  separate passes).
- `util/tests/test_regular_grid.py`: `regular_grid`.

## Dependencies and packaging

cuVS is not a required dependency of cuCIM: `slic` falls back to SciPy's `kmeans2` without it. It is
added to the test dependencies (`dependencies.yaml`, the conda environment files and the wheel
`test` extra in `pyproject.toml`) so that CI covers the cuVS path. The `cuvs-cu12` and `cuvs-cu13`
wheel versions are pinned to the RAPIDS version of the repository; the resolution of those wheels in
CI is worth watching.

title: regionprops: accurate `intensity_std` for large means
body:
## Summary

**This PR is stacked on the regionprops bug fixes in #1196 and the regionprops performance
improvements in #1198, in that order** (branch `grelee/regionprops-batch-perf`, which has the
kernels it changes: the intensity kernels of `_regionprops_gpu_intensity_kernels.py` and the label
run loop). Please review and merge those first; until they merge, this PR's diff also contains
their commits, so review only the last commit, "regionprops: compute intensity_std without
cancellation error".

The GPU `intensity_std` (and the `intensity_mean` that is returned with it) was computed in one pass
from the sums of the values and of their squares, as `sqrt((Σx² − mean²·n) / n)`. This subtracts two
nearly equal numbers when the mean is large compared with the standard deviation, so the relative
error of the result grows as eps · (mean / std)². With float64 sums that is 3e-7 at a mean-to-std
ratio of 1e4, 2e-3 at 1e6, and no correct digit at 1e8. Images with a large offset are common (for
example 16-bit microscopy images with a high background, or intensities in the thousands with a
standard deviation of a few units), and nothing warned about the loss. The old code carried a TODO
for it.

This PR computes the standard deviation accurately, and the cost is only paid when `intensity_std`
is requested. No other property depends on it: the mean, min, max and the other intensity
properties use the same code as before.

- **8 and 16-bit integer images (and bool):** the sums are exact integers, so `n·Σx² − (Σx)²`, which
  is `n²` times the variance, is evaluated exactly in 128-bit arithmetic. There is no extra pass and
  the time is unchanged.
- **Float images and wider integers:** a second pass over the image sums the deviations from the
  first-pass means, and the variance is `Σd² − (Σd)² / n` (the corrected two-pass algorithm). The
  first pass no longer accumulates squares. The error stays at 1e-14 or below in the table below
  however large the mean is, and the time is 1.4 to 2 times the old one.

## Changes

- `get_exact_mean_std_kernel`: the exact finalize for the integer sums. It uses `__umul64hi` and
  64-bit arithmetic for the 128-bit products instead of the `__int128` type (which needs
  `--device-int128` and is not available to NVRTC on Windows), so the same kernel compiles on every
  platform CuPy supports. `n·Σx² ≥ (Σx)²` (Cauchy-Schwarz), so the difference of the two 128-bit
  values needs no sign handling. The sum of squares of up to 2³² pixels of 16-bit values fits in
  64 bits, which is why this is used for 8 and 16-bit types only.
- `get_intensity_centered_kernel`: the second pass, built on the same label run loop and warp
  reduction as the first pass (one-channel images use the 16-byte reader, multi-channel images read
  each channel), accumulating `Σd` and `Σd²` in double precision. It does not read `means` for the
  background label.
- `get_mean_std_kernel`: finalizes the second-pass sums into the mean (`mean + Σd / n`, which also
  refines the mean) and the standard deviation.
- `get_mean_var_kernel` (the one-pass formula) is removed. The special cases are unchanged: a region
  with no pixel has a NaN std (population), a single pixel has std 0 (population) or NaN (sample),
  rounding that leaves a tiny negative variance gives 0 and not NaN, and a region with NaN or ±inf
  values has a NaN std.
- Fixes the message for a non-floating `std_dtype` (it said `mean_dtype`).

## Benchmarks

Measured on an RTX A6000, 4096 × 4096 label images with 4, 4096 and 65,536 square regions and
`regionprops_intensity_std` with the default parameters (GPU time, mean of 20 runs).

**Accuracy**: maximum relative error of `intensity_std` over four regions of 512 × 512 pixels,
against a `longdouble` two-pass reference. Normally distributed values with standard deviation 1
around a mean of `ratio`.

| mean / std | float64 before | float64 after | float32 before | float32 after |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1e2 | 2.4e-11 | 6.7e-16 | 1.1e-11 | 7.8e-16 |
| 1e4 | 2.5e-07 | 5.6e-16 | 9.4e-08 | 1.5e-14 |
| 1e6 | 2.1e-03 | 4.5e-16 | 8.1e-04 | 2.1e-14 |
| 1e8 | 5.6e+00 | 6.6e-16 | | |
| 1e10 | 5.1e+02 | 8.9e-16 | | |

For `uint16` images the error was 8.1e-10, 9.4e-08 and 7.4e-07 at ratios of 6e3, 6e4 and 2e5 and is
now 0 (equal to the correctly rounded reference).

**Time** (ms):

| Regions | dtype | before | after |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 4 | uint8 | 0.23 | 0.23 |
| 4 | uint16 | 0.23 | 0.23 |
| 4 | float32 | 0.41 | 0.79 |
| 4 | float64 | 0.36 | 0.73 |
| 4096 | uint8 | 0.20 | 0.20 |
| 4096 | uint16 | 0.21 | 0.21 |
| 4096 | float32 | 0.46 | 0.66 |
| 4096 | float64 | 0.33 | 0.67 |
| 65,536 | uint8 | 0.19 | 0.18 |
| 65,536 | uint16 | 0.21 | 0.20 |
| 65,536 | float32 | 0.32 | 0.60 |
| 65,536 | float64 | 0.34 | 0.65 |

The float cost is one more pass over the image, 1.4 to 2.0 times the one-pass time here. The 8 and
16-bit integer types do not pay anything.

I did not time the 32 and 64-bit integer types, which use the second pass like the float types.

## Behavior change

`intensity_std` (and `intensity_mean` when it is requested together with it) can differ from the
previous values by the old error: 2e-11 relative at a mean-to-std ratio of 1e2 in the table above,
and large for images with a large offset. Requests that do not include `intensity_std` are
unchanged.

## Testing

- `test_intensity_std_accuracy` (40 cases): dtypes `float64`, `float32`, `uint8`, `uint16`, `int16`,
  `int32`, `uint32`, `int64`, offsets that break the one-pass formula, one and three channels,
  population and sample standard deviation, a background label and regions of different sizes,
  against an extended precision reference (`rtol=1e-11`). On the old kernels 38 of the 40 fail.
- `test_intensity_std_exact_kernel_large_sums`: the exact kernel against Python integers for sums
  that use the full 128 bits (2³² − 1 pixels of 65535, negative sums, a variance of exactly 0).
- The existing intensity tests (including the constant-region and non-finite tests) pass unchanged.

This PR builds cuCIM as C++20 and replaces `fmt::format` with `std::format` in cuCIM's own sources, as #1191 proposes. The rest of RAPIDS and Holoscan already build as C++20.

Closes #1191.

## Who is affected

- **People who build cuCIM** need a C++20 compiler and a standard library with `<format>`, which GCC provides from version 13. The conda recipes pin GCC 14, and the CI wheel image uses `gcc-toolset-14`.
- **C++ code that uses the installed libcucim.** This change adds no C++20 or `<format>` requirement to the installed headers or to the exported `cucim::cucim` CMake target. No installed header changes, the headers keep using fmt, and the target still exports no C++ standard requirement.

## Commits

1. **Build with C++20.** Every first-party CMake project (libcucim, the GDS stub, the three plugins, the Python bindings, and their tests, benchmarks, and examples) moves from C++17 to C++20. The libcucim compile feature stays `PRIVATE`, as it was. Three small fixes keep the `-Werror` build passing:
   - `Timer::print` passes a runtime format string to `fmt::print`, which fmt only accepts through `fmt::runtime` in C++20 mode.
   - cuCIM's `libcuckoo.patch` replaces `std::is_pod`, which C++20 deprecates, with `std::is_standard_layout` and `std::is_trivial`.
   - cuslide2's `TIFF::construct_ifds` shrinks a non-empty vector with `erase` instead of `resize(1)`, which avoids a false GCC 14 `-Warray-bounds` error.
2. **Use std::format instead of fmt::format.** 161 calls in 34 files change. These stay on fmt:
   - `fmt::format` in the installed headers `cucim/util/cuda.h` and `cucim/memory/dlpack.h`, so consumers do not need `<format>`.
   - `fmt::print` and `fmt::join`, which have no C++20 equivalent.
   - One `fmt::format` call in cuslide2's `nvimgcodec_tiff_parser.cpp` that formats an `fmt::join` view.

   fmt therefore remains a dependency.

## Validation

The branch is based on `main` at `12e69a22`. All checks ran locally on x86_64 with GCC 14 and CUDA 13.3. CI has not run on this branch.

**Current commits (`6e6d49af`)**

These checks ran on `8054d80f`, which has the same file tree as `6e6d49af`. Only the commit email differs.

- **pre-commit.** `pre-commit run --hook-stage manual --all-files`, as CI runs it, passes.
- **Builds.** An incremental `./run build_local all release`, followed by every target in the five CMake trees, builds as C++20 with no errors. The 36 recompiled translation units give no warnings.
- **Tests.** The in-tree Python tests give 164 passed, 5 skipped.

**Earlier checks, before the rebase onto `main`.** These ran on the same two changes on top of #1188's branch (`17319017`) and were not repeated.

- **Builds.** A full build of all targets in the five CMake trees added no first-party warnings. It added 4 C++20 deprecation warnings from abseil in `_deps`.
- **C++ tests.** The four C++ test binaries gave the same assertion counts at base and after each commit. The same baseline failures recurred: tests that need test data not available locally, and an abort (SIGABRT) in cuslide2's `Verify read_region()` test case. On this machine the binaries hang at process exit after printing their results, on the base commit too.
- **Conda packages.** libcucim and cucim conda packages built with conda-build for CUDA 13.3, and libcucim also built for CUDA 12.9. The CUDA 13.3 cucim package passed `tests/unit` and `tests/performance` on Python 3.12 (164 passed, 5 skipped). `main` now builds the recipes with rattler-build, which was not run locally.
- **C++17 consumer.** A C++17 program that uses `find_package(cucim)` and links `cucim::cucim` compiled with `-std=c++17` against the C++20 build's install. It opened a TIFF and read a region, with output matching a build whose translation units preprocess identically to the base commit. The program also hung at process exit, as above.

Not covered: CI, wheel and manylinux artifacts, conda packages from the current commits, aarch64, CUDA 12 runtime tests, and compilers other than GCC 14. Seven converted calls are not compiled by any target: four in cuslide2's `tests/test_read_rawtiff.cpp`, which no CMake target lists, two in macro bodies in cuslide's `tests/test_read_rawtiff.cpp` that are never expanded, and one in cuslide2's `tiff/ifd.cpp`, in the branch for builds without nvImageCodec.

Closes #1192.

- 92 headers replace `#ifndef`/`#define`/`#endif` with `#pragma once`.

title: Fix `label2rgb` out-of-bounds GPU read when `bg_color=None`
body:
Closes #1233

`cucim.skimage.color.label2rgb(..., bg_color=None)` failed with `cudaErrorIllegalAddress`, with or without an image.

Cause: `_label2rgb_overlay` replaced `bg_color` by a zero-size array and only afterwards evaluated
`bg_color is None` to set `remove_background`, so that flag was always false. The kernels then read
`bg_color[0..2]` from the empty array for every background pixel.

Change: record `remove_background = bg_color is None` before `bg_color` is replaced, and use a 3-element zero array
as the placeholder. The background then shows the image, or stays zero when no image is given, as in scikit-image.
The `cp.any(label == bg_label)` reduction is no longer needed, because the kernel already checks each pixel.

Test: `test_bg_color_none` (with and without an image) in `color/tests/test_colorlabel.py`. On main both cases fail
with the CUDA error; with this change they pass, and `test_colorlabel.py` passes as a whole (30 passed). These runs
used one GPU, the `cucim-cu12` 26.10.0 wheel and the `cucim.skimage` sources of the branch placed over it, before the
branch was rebased onto the 27.02 version bump (version files only; not re-run after the rebase).

scikit-image, to write the fix and the test, to run the tests, and to draft this description. AI-generated code:

body:
## Description

Constrain CMake to `<4.5` in build dependencies and regenerate dependency files. CMake 4.5 exports CUDA link dependencies using `CUDAToolkit::` target names, which breaks consumers using older CMake versions.

Contributes to https://github.com/rapidsai/build-planning/issues/350.
